Article Title: AriGameplays shares heartbreaking message after Komanche’s death as his final X post goes viral
Article Text:
Image/Instagram

AriGameplays remembers Komanche in an emotional farewell message

“Komanche, nobody prepared me to live with the pain of no longer having you,”

“Many people didn't know you the way I did. You are an amazing person,”

“Every day I shared with you was a gift,”

“Rest in peace, my Komi. May God keep you in His glory. I will love and miss you all my life.”

Komanche’s final X post goes viral after his death

“The days just don't get any better.”

Twitch streamer AriGameplays has shared an emotional farewell to Komanche after the creator was found dead at his rental home in Monterrey, Mexico. Komanche, whose real name was Carlos Mauricio Gómez, died on October 25, according to reports. His death has left friends and fans heartbroken, especially after his final post on X gained millions of views. Ari remembered their close friendship in a long message on social media, saying that losing him had caused her deep pain.Ari shared a heartfelt letter on Instagram on October 27, remembering the happy moments they spent together and the special place he had in her life.she wrote. She also explained that many people did not know the person she knew privately.Ari added, praising him for supporting others even when he was dealing with his own problems.The streamer also revealed that her family in Monterrey had welcomed Komanche as one of their own. Over time, she began to see him as a brother.she wrote, expressing how thankful she was to have known him. She also remembered their final meeting and said she wished she had hugged him even more if she had known it would be their last time together.Ari ended her message with a loving goodbye, writing,Ari's emotional message came after Komanche's final post on X began spreading widely online. On October 19, the streamer wrote,The post later received more than nine million views, according to reports.The message has led fans to look back at his earlier comments about his personal struggles. Komanche had previously spoken about his mental health and his difficult experiences.Komanche was known for his funny videos, gaming streams and work on the Squid Craft Games, a Minecraft event inspired by the Netflix series Squid Game. He had built a large online following and was well known among Spanish-speaking gaming creators.Reports said he was found dead after neighbors noticed that the door of his rental home had been left open. Authorities in Nuevo León are investigating the circumstances surrounding his death, and the official cause has not been confirmed in the reports.Ari's farewell has now given fans another look at the friendship behind their online appearances.Komanche's death has left a painful loss for those who knew him personally and those who followed his work. Ari's message shows how much he meant to her and how deeply she will miss him.
Article Summary: Twitch streamer AriGameplays has shared an emotional farewell to Komanche. Komanche, whose real name was Carlos Mauricio Gómez, died on October 25. His death has left friends and fans heartbroken, especially after his final post on X gained millions of views.

Article Title: A Washington man rented an apartment beside a car-painting workshop where fumes made him ill; after a $95,904 damages judgment, an October 26 appeals court preserved $75,000 but overturned the extra d
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Paint fumes affected the rented apartment

Trial court awarded nearly $95,904

Appeals court upheld physical and emotional distress damages

Treble damages reversed, fee award sent back

Paint fumes drifting into a rented home can turn an ordinary tenancy into a question of health, safety and legal responsibility. In Redmond, Washington, tenant Eric Christiansen said fumes from an adjoining automobile-painting workshop made him ill and left his apartment uninhabitable. A trial court awarded him nearly $95,904 in damages after finding his landlords negligent and in violation of state landlord-tenant law. However, the Washington Court of Appeals, Division One, partly revised that outcome in an unpublished opinion issued on October 26, 2026, which does not constitute binding precedent. According to the ruling available on Justia , the court upheld $75,000 for physical pain and suffering and emotional distress but reversed the additional treble damages and ordered further proceedings on attorney fees.The dispute arose at a garage property owned by Larry Searles and associated with 938 164th Avenue, LLC. The facility in Redmond contained two apartments and an automobile workshop where Searles repaired and painted classic cars. Christiansen signed a two-year lease for one of the apartments on June 15, 2020. The other apartment was rented to Marshall Johnson, who worked as an automobile painter in the workshop. Although the workshop had a ventilation system and a paint booth, fumes and airborne particulates frequently accumulated when Johnson carried out painting work.Christiansen noticed the fumes entering his apartment on multiple occasions and began experiencing illness, physical pain and distress. On August 14, 2020, he complained to Searles that the fumes were making him sick. Three days later, Searles told him he would not be held to the lease if he wanted to leave. Christiansen also contacted King County about the conditions. On September 8, a county code enforcement officer inspected the property and determined that it was uninhabitable because of paint fumes and particulates in the air. The officer also identified missing occupancy permits. Both tenants were subsequently evicted, and Christiansen struggled to find alternative accommodation, affecting his eating habits and access to his mail.Christiansen sued Searles and the associated company, alleging negligence based on a breach of the implied warranty of habitability and violations of Washington's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act. Following a bench trial, the court found the defendants negligent and in violation of the legislation. It awarded Christiansen $25,000 for pain and suffering caused by physical illness and $50,000 for emotional distress, bringing the negligence damages to $75,000.The court separately calculated his actual damages under the landlord-tenant law at $6,967.99. It trebled that amount, producing an additional award of $20,903.97. Together, the two awards totalled $95,903.97, or approximately $95,904. The court also awarded reasonable attorney fees and litigation costs, to be determined separately. Christiansen initially sought nearly $98,465 in attorney fees but reduced his request to $76,710 after conceding certain objections raised by the defendants.Searles and the company challenged the damages award, arguing that Christiansen should not have received compensation for emotional distress without objective medical evidence of his symptoms. The appeals court rejected that argument. It explained that Washington law permits recovery for emotional distress accompanying a physical injury. The requirement for objective symptomatology, which generally applies to certain emotional distress claims without physical injury, did not apply in the same way here.The trial court had found that Christiansen experienced illness, including an upset stomach, after exposure to the fumes. Its findings also recorded his physical pain and emotional distress, supported by his credible testimony. Because those findings were not challenged on appeal, the appellate court accepted them. It concluded that the established physical illness meant Christiansen did not have to demonstrate objective symptomatology to recover the $50,000 emotional distress award. The $25,000 for physical pain and suffering also remained intact.The court reached a different conclusion on the additional damages awarded under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act. The relevant provision permits treble damages when a landlord knowingly violates specified statutory requirements, including conditions relating to the rental property's habitability. The appeals court found that the award could not stand because the statute required prior government notice that the dwelling had been condemned or was unlawful to occupy. Although Searles had avoided the permitting process during renovations, the record showed that no government entity had notified him of a relevant violation before he leased the apartment to Christiansen.The trial court had reasoned that notice was unnecessary because the landlord had deliberately avoided government authorities. The appeals court nevertheless reversed the treble damages award under the applicable statutory requirements. It also vacated the attorney fee award because the trial court had not provided sufficiently detailed findings and conclusions explaining its decision. The case was remanded for further proceedings, including a clearer explanation of the basis for attorney fees. The appeals court also denied Christiansen's request for attorney fees and costs on appeal.The ruling therefore preserved Christiansen's $75,000 award for physical pain and emotional distress while removing the additional $20,903.97 in treble damages. The fee issue remains subject to further proceedings in the trial court.
Article Summary: In Redmond, Washington, tenant Eric Christiansen said fumes from an adjoining automobile-painting workshop made him ill and left his apartment uninhabitable. A trial court awarded him nearly $95,904 in damages after finding his landlords negligent and in violation of state landlord-tenant law. However, the Washington Court of Appeals, Division One, partly revised that outcome in an unpublished opinion issued on October 26, 2026.

Article Title: Italian farmer planted mysterious seeds found in attic, discovered ancient biblical wheat with seven ears on one stalk that could help crops survive drought and climate change
Article Text:
Why the wheat reminded him of the Bible

A hardy crop with potential benefits

Could ancient wheat help agriculture adapt to climate change?

An Italian farmer who planted unidentified seeds found in his family’s attic ended up rediscovering a little-known heritage wheat variety that could offer useful lessons for agriculture facing climate change. As reported by Smithsonian Magazine, Claudio Grossi, a farmer near Parma in northern Italy, discovered that one of the plants growing from the seeds produced seven ears of grain on a single stalk, an unusual sight that reminded him of a passage in the Bible. The grain, later identified as Triticum turgidum, or poulard wheat, proved hardier than the commercial wheat varieties he was familiar with.The discovery dates back to the early 1990s, when Grossi was cleaning his attic and came across an old sack of seeds. He believed the bag had been left behind by his late great-grandfather, who established the family farm around 1915. The seeds were dry and cracked, and Grossi doubted they would grow. He carried them downstairs, scattered them over a pile of manure and forgot about them.But the seeds germinated, producing several kinds of wheat. One stood out immediately. Its plants grew to around six feet tall, roughly twice the height of typical commercial wheat, and developed a striking arrangement of seven ears: one long central ear surrounded by six shorter ones.The kernels were also larger than average and varied in colour, including yellow, black, red, white and green.“I thought it was a freak of nature,” Grossi told Smithsonian Magazine, explaining that he could not find a description of the unusual plant in the agricultural books he consulted.Grossi, a practising Catholic, found an unexpected parallel while reading the Book of Genesis. In the biblical account, Joseph interprets a dream experienced by the Egyptian pharaoh, in which seven full ears of grain grow on one stalk, followed by seven thin ears. The resemblance led Grossi to wonder whether the wheat he had grown might have ancient origins. However, the biblical connection was an inspiration for his investigation, not scientific proof that the plant came from biblical times.The identity of the grain was eventually established through food-science research. Beniamino Perobelli, then a student at the University of Parma, investigated its nutritional properties for his undergraduate thesis. Working with the laboratory of Teofilo Vamerali, a professor at the university, he identified the wheat as Triticum turgidum, commonly known as poulard wheat. The species originated in regions including present-day Turkey and Egypt and other parts of the Mediterranean, and historical references showed that it had also been cultivated in Italy before farmers moved towards higher-yielding commercial varieties.The likely explanation for the seeds surviving in the attic was therefore more practical than miraculous: Grossi’s great-grandfather had preserved seeds from an older farming tradition.Grossi began growing the wheat on his farm and called it grano del miracolo, Italian for “miracle grain”. He found that it performed better during droughts than the commercial wheat varieties he knew, grew tall enough to shade competing weeds and did not require the same reliance on fertilisers and herbicides.The crop also offered an unexpected nutritional profile. Research described by Smithsonian Magazine found that the wheat contained more phosphorus and iron than modern wheat varieties examined in the comparison. Researchers also reported lower gluten levels and the presence of amino acids such as lysine, tryptophan and arginine. These findings concern the grain studied and should not be taken to mean that it is safe for people with coeliac disease or that it is universally healthier than modern wheat.Turning the grain into bread, however, required experimentation. Grossi found that dough made from its flour did not rise as well as conventional wheat dough and tended to collapse. In the early 2000s, he began working with a local baker who preferred traditional hand-kneading methods. They experimented with smaller batches, taller wicker baskets and less kneading until the dough held its shape more successfully.Grossi described the resulting bread as rich and nutty, with a sweetness he felt was different from that of bread made with ordinary commercial flour. A local organic grain company, Molino Grassi, eventually began offering the flour to artisanal bakers, restaurants and consumers in Italy and abroad.The discovery has broader relevance because modern agriculture often depends on a relatively narrow selection of crop varieties. These varieties have helped increase food production, but relying heavily on a limited genetic pool can leave farming systems vulnerable to drought, extreme heat, plant diseases and pests.Francesco Sottile, an expert in agrosystem biodiversity at the University of Palermo, told Smithsonian Magazine that greater crop diversity can reduce this vulnerability. If one variety struggles under particular environmental conditions, another may still produce a harvest.He pointed to the severe drought experienced in Sicily in 2024, when many commercial wheat growers abandoned their fields before harvest. Some smaller farmers cultivating heritage grains were still able to collect their crops, he said. The example illustrates why traditional varieties may deserve further investigation, although it does not establish that every ancient wheat will outperform modern varieties under all conditions.The miracle wheat also has limitations. Its tall stems can be vulnerable to strong winds, heavy rain and hail, which may flatten plants before the grain ripens. Grossi addressed this problem by growing it alongside shorter wheat varieties that provide structural support.The discovery is therefore not proof that a single ancient grain can solve the climate crisis or replace modern wheat. Its importance lies in the genetic diversity and farming knowledge it brings back into consideration. As climate pressures intensify, studying heritage crops could help researchers and farmers identify useful traits for future breeding programmes.
Article Summary: Claudio Grossi, a farmer near Parma in northern Italy, discovered that one of the plants growing from the seeds produced seven ears of grain on a single stalk. The grain, later identified as Triticum turgidum, or poulard wheat, proved hardier than the commercial wheat varieties he was familiar with.

Article Title: Pakistan's gas mess: LPG prices soar, imported LNG piles up and the debt bill keeps growing
Article Text:
Expensive cylinders, dwindling reserves: Inside Pakistan's deepening gas crisis

A supply shock ahead of winter

First, understand the three fuels

Natural gas: Extracted from underground fields and delivered to homes, businesses and factories through pipelines. Pakistan's domestic production has been declining.

LNG: Natural gas cooled into liquid form for transport by ship. After arriving at a terminal, it is converted back into gas, known as regasified LNG or RLNG, and supplied through the network.

LPG: Liquefied petroleum gas, made up mainly of propane and butane. It is stored in cylinders and is especially important for households that do not have piped-gas connections.

Domestic gas is running out faster than new supplies are arriving

Pakistan's domestic gas production falls 20% in five years

The LNG paradox: Too little gas, then too much

A financial hole worth trillions

Pakistan's gas circular debt surges due to supply shortages

Why Pakistan's govt cannot simply raise prices

The crisis reaches far beyond the kitchen

Power sector, households, fertiliser and industry: Who consumes Pakistan's gas?

A domestic LPG cylinder that cost around PKR 4,500 in Pakistan's Balochistan province has shot up to nearly PKR 7,000. In some parts of the country, LPG prices have reached PKR 600 per kg, more than double the official rate. With supplies disrupted following the closure of key border crossings with Iran, households are struggling to find affordable cooking fuel. Some have even begun turning to wood and coal.But the shortage has exposed a much bigger problem. Pakistan's domestic natural gas production has been declining, its dependence on expensive imports has grown, and debts across its gas sector have reached trillions of rupees. Yet, even as households struggle with shortages, the country has also been dealing with surplus imported LNG that it cannot easily use or sell.On October 21, 2026, Dawn reported that LPG prices had climbed to as much as PKR 600 per kg in hilly areas and PKR 500 per kg in Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, even though the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) had fixed the official October rate at around PKR 279 per kg. The regulator's notified price for an 11.8kg domestic cylinder was PKR 3,296.23.The disruption has since intensified. Reuters reported on October 23 that the closure of the Gabd-Rimdan and Taftan crossings with Iran had halted LPG imports, leaving tankers stranded and worsening shortages.Traders said Pakistan imported about 7,000 metric tonnes of LPG a day from Iran. In Balochistan, the price of a 12kg cylinder had risen from around PKR 4,500 to PKR 7,000. Pakistan cited security and anti-smuggling concerns for the border closure, while Iran pointed to technical issues. The two sides were consulting on resuming trade.The pressure is also visible in Rawalpindi and Islamabad. Dawn reported on October 26 that households facing limited piped-gas supply and soaring LPG prices had begun turning to wood and coal for cooking. Residents reported receiving natural gas for only about six hours a day, while LPG was selling at around PKR 600 per kg.Part of the confusion around Pakistan's gas crisis comes from the fact that three different fuels are often discussed as though they are interchangeable.The distinction matters because a disruption in one supply chain does not automatically mean the same thing for the others.The fuels nevertheless compete for the same household energy budget. When piped gas is unavailable or supplied only for a few hours, families turn to LPG. When LPG becomes unaffordable, some shift to wood or coal. The result is that a supply shock in one part of the system can quickly affect everyday life.The Pakistan Institute of Development Economics (PIDE), a government-backed research institution, said domestic gas production fell from 3,597 million cubic feet per day in financial year 2020 to 2,890 million cubic feet per day in FY2025. That is a decline of nearly 20% in five years. PIDE attributed the fall to the depletion of mature fields and a failure of new discoveries to replace the lost output.The Pakistan Economic Survey 2024-25 offers another snapshot of the pressure on the system. It recorded average gas consumption of 3,143 million cubic feet per day during July-March FY2025, including 798 million cubic feet per day of imported RLNG. Domestic gas remained crucial, but imported supplies were already filling a substantial part of the gap.This is not simply a matter of turning up production. Gas exploration requires investment, time and confidence that companies will be paid for what they produce. PIDE has argued that payment delays, distorted price signals and the financial troubles of state-owned gas utilities have weakened incentives for investment. It has also highlighted the damage caused when domestic production is curtailed to make room for imported LNG.Pakistan began importing LNG in 2015 as domestic production became insufficient. Its supply arrangements include long-term contracts with Qatar, one lasting 15 years and another 10 years, as well as an agreement with Italy's Eni. These contracts helped secure supplies, but they also reduced the government's flexibility when demand changed.The problem became particularly visible in 2025. According to the US-based Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), LNG consumption fell by 1.21 million tonnes that year. Rapid growth in rooftop solar power and weaker demand from the electricity grid contributed to a change in the country's energy requirements.Yet contracted LNG supplies could not be adjusted easily enough to reflect the fall in demand.That left Pakistan facing an unusual predicament: A country struggling with gas shortages could also have more imported LNG than it needed at particular times.With limited storage capacity, surplus LNG had to be diverted into the domestic network or otherwise managed. But imported gas costs more than much of Pakistan's domestically produced gas, while household tariffs have often been kept below the full cost of supply.Diverting expensive imported fuel to consumers at lower regulated rates can therefore create losses rather than solve the underlying financial problem.IEEFA estimated that Pakistan's gas-sector circular debt stood at around PKR 3.3 trillion in its March 2026 assessment. The think tank also said unaccounted-for gas losses, including theft and technical leakages, were estimated at around 11.7% of gas handled.On October 20, Business Recorder reported that federal energy minister Ali Pervaiz Malik had told the National Assembly that Pakistan's total gas-sector circular debt and outstanding payments to domestic gas and LNG suppliers stood at PKR 5.454 trillion as of June 30, 2026.Of this, circular debt accounted for PKR 3.631 trillion, while outstanding payments to gas suppliers amounted to another PKR 1.823 trillion. The minister said the circular debt included PKR 1.448 trillion in tariff differentials, PKR 131 billion in receivables from power companies, PKR 210 billion in sales and income tax receivables, and PKR 59 billion related to litigation.Circular debt builds up when money owed at one point in the supply chain is not paid on time, preventing the next entity from meeting its own obligations. In Pakistan's gas sector, the problem has been aggravated by tariff gaps, unpaid bills, delayed payments and the cost of imported fuel.The consequences extend beyond balance sheets. When gas utilities struggle to recover the cost of supply, their ability to pay producers and maintain infrastructure comes under pressure. Producers, in turn, have less incentive to invest in new fields. Consumers may face higher tariffs, restricted supply or both.The IMF's concerns have continued into 2026. Dawn reported on October 2 that the lender had urged Pakistan to speed up work on targeted gas subsidies and address the sector's rising circular debt. The report said discussions were under way on shifting support from subsidised tariffs towards direct assistance for eligible low-income households, although data and ownership-related problems made the transition difficult.Pakistan's government has tried to balance financial reform with relief for consumers. On January 6, 2026, the Press Information Department reported that petroleum minister Ali Pervaiz Malik had announced, on PM Shehbaz Sharif's directions, that gas prices would remain unchanged for six months.The minister also said the government had negotiated with Qatar to divert surplus LNG cargoes to international markets while respecting contractual obligations.But holding tariffs steady does not automatically eliminate the gap between what gas costs and what consumers pay. Nor does it address the separate problem of LPG prices in the open market, where supply disruptions can push prices well above the regulator's notified rate.The Shehbaz Sharif-led government has also considered replacing broad gas subsidies with a single fair price, while protecting vulnerable households through targeted assistance. On August 27, the detroleum division said petroleum minister Ali Pervaiz Malik had urged reforms, including steps to curb gas theft, reduce losses and improve revenue recovery at Sui Southern Gas Company.Pakistan's Economic Survey for 2024-25 recorded average daily gas consumption of 3,143 million cubic feet during July-March FY2025. The power sector accounted for 973 million cubic feet per day, while domestic consumers used 777 million and the fertiliser sector 764 million. General industry consumed another 536 million cubic feet per day.These figures show why gas allocation is such a difficult policy choice. A supply shortfall can affect household cooking and heating, but it can also disrupt electricity generation, fertiliser production and industrial operations.Fertiliser plants are particularly important because their output feeds directly into agriculture. If gas supply or prices disrupt production, the effects can spread through fertiliser availability, farming costs and food prices. Industries that depend on gas for heat, processing or captive power can also face higher costs, potentially weakening competitiveness and investment.Until those structural problems are addressed, temporary relief may ease one winter's hardship without preventing the next shortage. Pakistan's gas crisis is bigger than LPG prices because the cylinder is only where a much wider failure becomes visible.
Article Summary: Pakistan's domestic natural gas production has been declining. Its dependence on expensive imports has grown. The country's debts across its gas sector have reached trillions of rupees. A domestic LPG cylinder that cost around PKR 4,500 in Balochistan province has shot up to nearly PKR 7,000.

Article Title: In 1924, a Wisconsin farmer began transforming his new home into a world of carved birds and painted figures, creating Bird’s Park, an unusual art environment now recreated in a museum
Article Text:
PC: John Michael Kohler Arts Center

How Albert Zahn turned woodworking into Bird’s Park

The wider collection behind Zahn’s bird carvings

How Zahn’s work entered museum collections

The place that remains in Baileys Harbor

In 1924, Wisconsin farmer Albert Zahn moved into a house he had built in Baileys Harbor and began filling it with carved birds, angels and wooden figures. His wife, Louise, painted the creations, turning their home into Bird’s Park, a local attraction that drew visitors for years. Although the original art environment has since been dismantled, the house still stands and many of the carvings survive. The Kohler Foundation acquired numerous pieces, while the John Michael Kohler Arts Center in Sheboygan preserves a substantial collection and recreates elements of Zahn’s unusual home at its Art Preserve.Zahn’s route to carving began long before he settled in Baileys Harbor. Born in 1864 in what is now north-western Poland, he emigrated to Wisconsin with his family as a teenager. He later recalled whittling wood while working as a shepherd in Europe. In Wisconsin, he became a dairy farmer and raised a large family with Louise, whom he married in 1891.Woodworking was initially part of everyday life. Timber from the surrounding area supplied material for practical household pieces, including tables, dressers and wardrobes. Zahn decorated some of these objects with birds and other creatures, imagery that gradually became the centre of his artistic work.In 1924, the family left its farm and moved to a house Zahn built from concrete blocks in Baileys Harbor, on the Door County shoreline. There, carving occupied much of his time. He produced birds, woodland animals, angels and figures drawn from local stories. Louise painted the wooden forms, using ordinary house paint to give them colour.By the early 1930s, the house and its grounds had become crowded with carved creatures. Birds appeared in groups and on structures around the property, creating an environment that was as much about their arrangement as the individual objects. Locals knew the place as Bird’s Park, and visitors came to see it while Zahn was still alive. He died in 1953; Louise had died three years earlier in 1950.Birds became Zahn’s best-known subject, but his work extended into other forms. He carved angels, sailors and sea captains, as well as ships, whirligigs and pieces of furniture. One recurring motif was the bird tree, a sculptural arrangement in which multiple birds occupied the branches of a single form.The objects reflect both sides of Zahn’s working life. Some pieces grew out of his experience making furniture for a household and farm; others were created for display, with painted figures and unusual shapes turning familiar materials into something more elaborate. His wife’s contribution was important to the finished appearance of the work. Zahn carved the forms, while Louise painted many of them, helping establish the bright look associated with Bird’s Park.The house still stands, but the collection that once covered its exterior and grounds was dispersed and the setting dismantled. Individual carvings, furniture and other objects survived, however, and later collectors and institutions worked to bring pieces together.The Kohler Foundation has acquired numerous works by Zahn through relatives and private collectors. The collection includes birds and other carved figures, a ship, a rooster weathervane, a bird tree and a rocking chair, alongside furniture and other objects. Their condition varied. Some needed substantial conservation, while others required little more than cleaning and minor stabilisation.As reported by Kohler Foundation, conservation work was carried out by Megan Thumm Mackey, a conservator based in Madison, Wisconsin. Such work helped prepare pieces for continued care and public display, particularly where age or earlier conditions had left the wood and painted surfaces in need of attention.The John Michael Kohler Arts Center in Sheboygan holds a substantial collection of Zahn’s work. In 2003, the centre organised a major exhibition that brought together more than 200 pieces from around the country. The show offered visitors a chance to see the range of his carving, beyond the birds that made his name locally.The house Zahn called Bird’s Park remains at the north end of Baileys Harbor, a physical reminder of the place where he and Louise assembled their unusual display. The carvings that once filled its exterior and grounds are no longer gathered there, so the building and the surviving collection now tell different parts of the story.Zahn’s work is preserved across collections rather than within the original setting alone. The Art Preserve’s reconstruction helps explain how the objects related to one another, while individual pieces document the details of his carving and Louise’s painting. Together, they offer a record of an art environment built gradually by a farmer and his wife in Door County.
Article Summary: Wisconsin farmer Albert Zahn built a house in Baileys Harbor in 1924. He filled it with carved birds, angels and wooden figures. His wife, Louise, painted the creations, turning their home into Bird’s Park. Although the original art environment has since been dismantled, the house still stands and many of the carvings survive.

Article Title: A federal judge ruled Trump-appointed prosecutor Bill Essayli is unlawfully serving as Los Angeles's top U.S. attorney and disqualified him from two cases, but paused the disqualification while the Ju
Article Text:
Bill Essayli Photo credit: REUTERS/Daniel Cole

What the ruling means

Why the appointment is contested

A wider fight over prosecutors

Note: This article is based on the court’s October 27, 2026 order. The government may still seek a stay, which could change how and when the ruling takes effect.

A federal judge has ruled that Bill Essayli has been serving unlawfully as Los Angeles’ top federal prosecutor. The ruling represents a legal setback for the Justice Department’s effort to preserve Essayli’s authority, but it does not immediately remove Essayli from his position. Senior U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright instead temporarily delayed the practical effect of his ruling, giving federal prosecutors five business days to ask for a stay while they pursue an appeal. The ruling was reported by the Los Angeles Times, The Guardian and CBS News Los Angeles, all of which describe a court order that challenges the legal arrangement used to keep Essayli in charge of one of the nation’s largest federal judicial districts.The dispute centers on Essayli’s authority to lead the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California, which covers Los Angeles and six other counties. Judge Seabright concluded that Essayli is unlawfully serving as a “de facto” United States attorney, even though his official title is first assistant U.S. attorney. In practical terms, the judge found that the Justice Department gave Essayli powers so broad that he effectively occupied the top job without holding it lawfully.“In sum, Essayli is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney,” Seabright wrote, according to the Los Angeles Times.The ruling does not mean Essayli has been removed from office today. Judge Seabright ordered that Essayli be disqualified from participating in or supervising two criminal prosecutions, including overseeing the lawyers working on those matters. However, the judge paused that disqualification while the government prepares its expected request for a stay pending appeal. CBS News reported that the government has five business days to file that request, and that the disqualifications would take effect one week later if the request is denied, unless a higher court intervenes.The two cases affected involve Jaime Hector Ramirez , who is charged with being a felon in possession of a firearm and ammunition, and Tu Anh Tran, who is charged with possessing property stolen from interstate or foreign shipment. Judge Seabright barred Essayli from taking part in or supervising those prosecutions. That means he cannot direct the attorneys handling the cases or otherwise exercise authority over them while the disqualification remains in place. The Los Angeles Times and CBS News both reported that the judge rejected requests to dismiss the indictments against Ramirez and Tran.That distinction matters. The judge found a problem with Essayli’s authority, but he did not conclude that the underlying criminal cases must collapse. Seabright said the defendants had not shown the substantial prejudice needed to justify dismissing the indictments. In other words, the ruling removes Essayli from a supervisory role in two prosecutions, but it leaves the charges themselves intact for now.Essayli responded to the decision by saying that his office respectfully disagreed with the order. He argued that the president and attorney general have the right to choose supervisors within the Justice Department. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court , and I look forward to serving in my current role until then,” Essayli said, according to CBS News. His comments make clear that the administration views the issue as far from settled and expects it to move toward the nation’s highest court.The legal fight began after Essayli was sworn in as interim U.S. attorney for the Central District of California in April 2025. When he approached the 120-day limit for serving in that temporary role, he resigned and was then appointed by Attorney General Pam Bondi as a special attorney and first assistant U.S. attorney. The Justice Department used that arrangement to allow him to continue leading the office as acting U.S. attorney. The Los Angeles Times reported that Judge Seabright rejected a similar maneuver last year, though he initially allowed Essayli to keep supervising prosecutions in his other roles.The Justice Department later revised Essayli’s delegation of authority, excluding certain powers that federal law reserves for a Senate-confirmed U.S. attorney. Government lawyers argued that this change placed Essayli’s authority on the permissible side of the legal line. Judge Seabright was not persuaded. He found that the revision made no meaningful difference because the withheld powers could not lawfully have been delegated to Essayli in the first place. “Withholding the three specific statutory powers mentioned in the revised designation order in reality withholds nothing,” the judge wrote, according to the Los Angeles Times.The ruling also follows a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit in a similar Nevada case involving prosecutor Sigal Chattah. That appeals court held that the Justice Department cannot keep an unconfirmed official in charge of a U.S. attorney’s office simply by changing the person’s title while giving them the full powers of the job. The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to review the Nevada decision, arguing that federal law permits the attorney general to delegate the powers of a vacant office and install a first assistant as its acting leader. The Supreme Court has not yet said whether it will hear the case.The Los Angeles case is part of a broader national dispute over how the Trump administration has installed chosen prosecutors without Senate confirmation. The Los Angeles Times noted that former New Jersey prosecutor Alina Habba stepped down after an appeals court found her appointment unlawful. In Virginia, a judge’s finding that Lindsey Halligan was unlawfully appointed led to the dismissal of indictments against former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Those cases have made the question of temporary prosecutor appointments unusually consequential.For now, the immediate consequence in Los Angeles is narrow but consequential. Essayli remains in his role, but a federal judge has found that his authority to lead the office is legally flawed. If the government fails to obtain a stay, he will be barred from the Ramirez and Tran cases, although the office itself will continue operating. The Los Angeles Times reported that President Trump had still not nominated anyone to serve as U.S. attorney for the Central District of California as of Tuesday’s ruling.Defense lawyer H. Dean Steward, who filed a renewed challenge to Essayli’s authority in August, welcomed the ruling. He called it “a victory for the rule of law and the U.S. Constitution” and accused the Trump administration of ignoring the laws governing the appointment of U.S. attorneys. His comments, reported by the Los Angeles Times, reflect the view of critics who say the administration has used title changes and delegated authority to avoid the Senate confirmation process.The next step will determine whether the disqualification takes effect in the two cases, while the broader question of Essayli’s authority to lead the office remains contested. The Justice Department can ask Judge Seabright to stay the disqualification while it appeals, and the case may ultimately reach the Supreme Court alongside the related Nevada dispute. Until then, the ruling leaves unresolved whether a revised title and delegated authority can lawfully sustain Essayli’s leadership of the office. The Los Angeles Times, The Guardian and CBS News all frame the decision as part of an unresolved constitutional battle over who may lead federal prosecutor offices and under what legal authority.
Article Summary: A federal judge has ruled that Bill Essayli has been serving unlawfully as Los Angeles’ top federal prosecutor. The ruling represents a legal setback for the Justice Department’s effort to preserveEssayli’S authority, but it does not immediately remove him from his position. The government may still seek a stay, which could change how and when the ruling takes effect.

Article Title: A rare gold coin from the reign of England’s Edward III, minted as a ‘leopard’ that was in circulation for just seven months in the 14th century, emerged from an ordinary suburban home and has sold at
Article Text:
Why Edward III introduced the gold leopard

A currency experiment that lasted only months

A rare survivor attracts collectors

A rare 14th-century English gold coin that circulated for only seven months has sold for £70,000 at auction, after emerging from an ordinary suburban home. According to Antiques Trade Gazette, the coin, known as a leopard and issued during the reign of King Edward III, was sold by Essex Coin Auctions on September 30, 2026, attracting competing bids from online and telephone buyers. Two telephone bidders contested the lot in the final stages, pushing it to its reported hammer price of £70,000.The coin’s short time in circulation is central to its historical significance. Edward III, who ruled England from 1327 to 1377, introduced a series of gold coins in 1344 as England sought to strengthen its own currency and support trade. The experiment included the double leopard, leopard and half-leopard. However, the coins were abandoned within months and replaced by a different gold denomination, the noble.The British Museum’s historical record explains that England’s move towards gold coinage was driven partly by the needs of international commerce. During the 1340s, gold coins from France and Florence were already widely used, and England wanted its own currency to play a stronger role in trade. Parliament petitioned Edward III to introduce gold coins, with the new denominations ordered in December 1343.The designs also carried political meaning. According to the British Museum, the gold florin featured the king seated with an orb and sceptre, flanked by two heraldic English leopards. A Gothic canopy and fleurs-de-lis appeared in the design, while the inscription included Edward’s claim to the French throne. These elements reflected the political ambitions that formed part of the backdrop to the Hundred Years’ War between England and France.The name “leopard” referred to the heraldic animals depicted on the coinage. The denominations included a double leopard, also known as a double florin, alongside the smaller leopard and half-leopard. The coins were made of gold and represented an effort to establish an English alternative to foreign currency used by merchants.Despite the ambition behind the launch, the leopard coinage proved unsuccessful. The British Museum notes that the new currency was overvalued, meaning its face value was higher than the value of the gold it contained. Its denominations also did not fit comfortably into England’s existing monetary system, making the coins less practical for everyday use.The Numismatic Guaranty Company (NGC), an organisation specialising in coin grading and authentication, says Edward III’s gold leopard coinage was struck between January and July 1344. The coins were then abandoned in favour of the gold noble, which became a more successful denomination. The leopard coins were officially demonetised on August 20, 1344.The noble was valued at six shillings and eight pence, equivalent to a third of a pound. The Royal Mint’s historical guide describes it as the first English gold coin to become firmly established in circulation. It was issued alongside half-nobles and quarter-nobles, and its design and usefulness helped it remain in circulation for far longer than the short-lived leopard series.The leopard’s brief lifespan helps explain its rarity today. NGC notes that relatively few gold leopard coins were struck and that many were probably melted down after the currency was withdrawn. Coins that survived the transition are now important examples of an early attempt to introduce a lasting English gold currency.The £70,000 sale reported by Antiques Trade Gazette illustrates the interest that such surviving pieces can attract in the collectables market. The publication reported that the coin was offered by Essex Coin Auctions on September 30, with a 22% buyer’s premium applying to the sale. It described the £70,000 result as the hammer price, so the figure should not automatically be treated as the buyer’s total bill after the premium.The report said bidding came from both online and telephone participants, with two telephone bidders competing towards the end. The coin’s emergence from a suburban home adds an unexpected element to the story, although the available report does not establish further details about the circumstances of its discovery. It would therefore be inaccurate to assume that it was found by a metal detectorist or to attribute a specific discovery date without additional evidence.Other surviving coins from Edward III’s gold coinage have also drawn attention. NGC records that two examples of the double leopard were found in the River Tyne by schoolchildren in 1857 and later entered the British Museum’s collection. A third known example was discovered by a metal detectorist in southern England in 2006 and sold at auction that year. These are separate coins from the one reported in the 2026 Essex auction.The British Museum’s records provide a further reminder of the coinage’s historical importance: Edward III’s gold florin was part of an attempt to support trade and strengthen the kingdom’s monetary system, even though the initial design and valuation failed to win lasting acceptance.
Article Summary: The coin was sold by Essex Coin Auctions on September 30, 2026. It attracted competing bids from online and telephone buyers. Two telephone bidders contested the lot in the final stages, pushing it to its reported hammer price of £70,000. The coin’s short time in circulation is central to its historical significance.

‘This is not your communist dictatorship’: US, Cuban envoys clash at UN

Article Title: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil after Lula defeat, US offers visas to family
Article Text:
Flavio Bolsonaro flew to US after electoral defeat

Brazilian senator Flavio Bolsonaro has fled to the United States after losing the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. He is reportedly in Miami with his family, while the US state department is set to issue entry visas to them.Bolsonaro’s departure came after he failed to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports within 24 hours. The court had ordered the passports seized over a money laundering probe, in which Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing, citing concerns that he could flee Brazil and his “significant financial resources”. Two sources told Reuters that his passports were cancelled after the deadline expired.The location of Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters was not immediately clear. A source close to the family told Reuters that he had landed in Florida but declined to specify where. BBC report suggests that Bolsonaro is in Miami.“The State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States,” a senior US State Department official told Reuters.Bolsonaro’s departure could deepen tensions between Washington and Brasil. Lula has accused the US of colluding with the Bolsonaro family to bring them back to power.US president Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio’s father, was the target of judicial persecution. Trump also said on Monday that Brazil’s election “looked like another rigged election”, without providing evidence in the remarks cited by Reuters.Lula, speaking in Brasilia, said he had just learned of Flavio’s departure and called it shameful, arguing that the senator should have stayed in Brazil to prove his innocence.Flavio Bolsonaro has yet to formally concede defeat. On Sunday, he said he would seek to annul the election result over alleged voter irregularities, although his Liberal Party said on Monday that it acknowledged Lula’s victory.The circumstances of his departure remain unclear. A senior Brazilian federal police official told Reuters that Bolsonaro had not left the country through any regular migration point.On Monday, Bolsonaro had denied any intention of fleeing Brazil, saying he would surrender his passports and defend himself against what he called an attempt to intimidate him. His campaign manager, senator Rogerio Marinho, said he was surprised by reports of the departure, adding that they had discussed Bolsonaro taking on the role of opposition leader after receiving about 60 million votes.Bolsonaro is due to lose his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February. His departure also echoes that of his father, who went to the United States after refusing to concede defeat to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro later returned to Brazil and was sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
Article Summary: Brazilian senator Flavio Bolsonaro has fled to the United States after losing the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. He is reportedly in Miami with his family, while the US state department is set to issue entry visas to them. His departure came after he failed to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports within 24 hours.

Article Title: Netanyahu seeks 'right-wing, national, strong government' in tight Israel election race
Article Text:
Israeli Prime Minister and Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu

Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has claimed that his right-wing bloc secured a “clear, decisive majority” and called for a “right-wing, national, strong government”, even as exit polls suggested that neither his camp nor the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot had secured the 61 seats required to form a majority in the 120-member Knesset.In his first reaction to the exit poll projections, Netanyahu addressed supporters at Likud’s election headquarters in Jerusalem, saying his party remained Israel’s largest political force and insisting that the right-wing bloc had enough support to govern.“What we’ve seen is that the Likud party is the largest party and nobody can compete with us,” he said. “The second thing that is clear as well is that the right block has a majority. And it is a decisive majority.”“We need to form a national right-wing government,” he added, arguing that Israel should not depend on Arab-led parties, which he described as being “against our existence”.Netanyahu also criticised television channels for projecting stronger results for opposition parties and accused them of discouraging his supporters from voting. He attacked what he called “criminal political investigations” into him.Turning to Iran, Netanyahu said Israel was facing a significant strategic opportunity alongside Washington.“Iran is weaker than ever, Israel is stronger than ever,” he said. “Israel is facing a historic, one-time opportunity along with our friend President Trump” to “remove the Iranian threat once and for all”.He also said, “We have been able to overcome our enemies, and we will be able to in the future.”The prime minister’s claims came after exit polls released by major Israeli television stations projected around 51 seats each for Netanyahu’s bloc and Eisenkot’s camp, with Arab-led parties winning about 18 seats. The projections remain preliminary and could change as official counting progresses.The vote count has already begun. Once counting at polling stations is complete, officials will turn to the “double envelopes” - ballots cast by soldiers, diplomats, doctors and nurses who cannot leave their posts to vote in person. Around 600,000 such envelopes are in the count, and while they do not usually alter the overall outcome significantly, shifting exit polls have added to the uncertainty.Netanyahu’s Likud could emerge as the largest single party, but the broader political arithmetic leaves the formation of a government uncertain. His coalition, which previously had 68 members, had weakened over the past year amid disagreements, including over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews.Eisenkot, meanwhile, said the exit polls indicated a “lack of confidence” in Netanyahu and pledged to form a government.“Today, Israel went out to a referendum over the leadership that will lead Israel in the coming years,” he said. “The people decided in favor of change.”Promising “a new era — an era of hope”, Eisenkot warned Netanyahu not to “dare use Israel’s security for your political needs” while serving as caretaker prime minister.Turnout exceeded 77 per cent, the highest since 1999, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee. The president will now be tasked with identifying the party leader best placed to assemble a governing coalition.
Article Summary: Netanyahu claims his right-wing bloc secured a ‘clear, decisive majority’ Neither his camp nor the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot had secured the 61 seats required to form a majority in the 120-member Knesset. Turnout exceeded 77 per cent, the highest since 1999.

Article Title: A Georgia winery owner challenged rezoning of 114 neighbouring acres for dense housing over traffic, noise and runoff; an October 27 appeals court reversed a lower-court ruling in the dispute with Hal
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Rezoning proposal prompted legal challenge

Case returned from federal court

Appeals court examined sovereign immunity

Earlier dismissal of officials did not resolve the issue

A proposed housing development can raise concerns about more than just the number of homes planned for a neighbourhood. For a Georgia winery owner, the rezoning of approximately 114 acres of neighbouring land prompted fears about traffic congestion, noise, water runoff and the potential impact on his business. The dispute reached the state’s Court of Appeals after the Hall County Board of Commissioners approved the rezoning for a planned residential development. According to the court’s October 27, 2026, opinion, available on Justia in Hall County v. Faul, the appeals court reversed a lower court’s refusal to grant summary judgment to the county and its Board of Commissioners, finding that the lawsuit failed to meet a constitutional requirement governing such challenges.The dispute began in 2024, when several property owners applied to Hall County to rezone approximately 114 acres from agricultural residential use to a planned residential development. The application sought to permit high-density housing on the property. Mark Douglas Faul, who owns Arrowquest Services Inc., operates a winery on a 2.21-acre property in Hall County. He joined other property owners in opposing the rezoning, which the Hall County Board of Commissioners ultimately approved.The opponents subsequently filed a petition in the Superior Court of Hall County seeking judicial review of the zoning decision. They named the county, its Board of Commissioners, several county officials and the owners of the land subject to rezoning as respondents. The petitioners argued that the development could harm nearby properties and businesses. Their stated concerns included potential losses in business income and property values, heavy traffic, noise, odours, mosquitoes associated with planned retention ponds, water runoff and intrusions on privacy.They also raised constitutional claims involving due process, equal protection and the taking of property without just and adequate compensation. They asked the court to reverse the rezoning, declare the decision void and issue temporary and permanent injunctions, along with awarding damages and attorney fees.The respondents initially removed the dispute to the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia because the petition included claims under the US Constitution. However, the case was subsequently returned to the state court after the petitioners dismissed their federal constitutional claims. Back in the Superior Court of Hall County, the private landowners sought judgment on the pleadings, arguing that the lawsuit should be dismissed because it did not comply with a provision of the Georgia Constitution governing actions against state and local governments.The petitioners then sought to dismiss the county employees named in the case. The trial court granted that request and concluded that removing those officials remedied the problem with the lawsuit's party structure. However, the Board of Commissioners and the private landowners remained defendants. Hall County and the board subsequently sought summary judgment, arguing that sovereign immunity continued to protect them from the lawsuit. The trial court denied the motion, allowing the challenge to proceed. The county and the board appealed that decision to the Georgia Court of Appeals.The central question before the appeals court was not whether the proposed housing development would cause the alleged environmental or neighbourhood impacts. Instead, the judges examined whether the lawsuit complied with the constitutional requirements for challenging government actions through a request for declaratory relief.The court explained that Georgia's Constitution provides a limited waiver of sovereign immunity for certain lawsuits seeking a declaration that a government action was unlawful or unconstitutional. However, a case relying on that provision must be brought exclusively against the relevant local government, and naming unauthorised additional defendants can require dismissal of the entire lawsuit.The judges noted that the petitioners had asked the court to declare the rezoning decision void. By seeking that relief, they were relying at least partly on the constitutional waiver of sovereign immunity. Consequently, the lawsuit could not continue while retaining the Board of Commissioners and the private landowners as additional defendants.The petitioners argued that naming additional parties was a procedural defect that could be corrected by removing those defendants rather than dismissing the entire case. They relied on an earlier Georgia Supreme Court decision recognising that such naming errors could be cured.The appeals court distinguished that precedent. In the earlier case, the plaintiff had sought to remove the individual defendants before the lawsuit was dismissed. In the Hall County dispute, however, the petitioners removed only the county employees while leaving their claims against the Board of Commissioners and the private landowners pending. The judges concluded that the petitioners had not corrected the defect. Because the lawsuit relied on the constitutional waiver but failed to meet its exclusivity requirement, dismissal was warranted.The Court of Appeals therefore reversed the trial court's denial of summary judgment. It did not decide whether the proposed development would cause the alleged traffic, noise, runoff or financial harms, nor did it resolve the county's remaining arguments. The October 27 ruling addressed the legal requirements governing the challenge, rather than the merits of the rezoning itself.
Article Summary: Rezoning proposal prompted legal challenge. Case returned from federal court.Appeals court examined sovereign immunity. Earlier dismissal of officials did not resolve the issue. The October 27 ruling addressed the legal requirements rather than the merits of the rezoning itself.

Article Title: In 2003, Alicia Keys co-founded a charity to help children affected by HIV; two decades later, it has raised $86.6 million and supports 9.3 million children, young people and families in 28 countries
Article Text:
A trip that changed many lives

Keep a Child Alive

Alicia Keys, 45, is now a mother of five (two biological children and three stepchildren). Motherhood came to her as an adult, but the instinct to look after children was there well before that. Long before she had children of her own, she was already caring about children on the brink of neglect.Alicia Keys was just 20 when she travelled to South Africa as part of MTV’s Staying Alive campaign. During the visit, she went to clinics where pregnant women and new mothers were confronting the reality of HIV/AIDS, including the risk of passing the virus on to their babies. She also witnessed widows and children orphaned by AIDS struggling to survive. “I couldn’t turn my back on all I’d seen,” Keys told WebMD at the time. The experience inspired her to co-found Keep a Child Alive in 2003 alongside AIDS activist Leigh Blake, with the aim of helping children and families affected by HIV/AIDS access life-saving medication and essential support.Twenty years later, the non-profit charity had raised $86.6 million, worked in 28 countries and supported over 9.3 million children, young people and families.At 20, Keys travelled to South Africa as part of MTV’s Staying Alive campaign, which focused on HIV and AIDS. What she saw there changed her life and many others for the better. “At the time, a lot of women didn’t realize that if you are positive and you breastfeed your baby, your baby will contract it,” Keys told People in 2019. “The moms just wanted medicine to keep them alive. That was the first time as a 20-year-old that I was aware of the injustice. I thought, ‘How can something be available, but you can’t have it because you’re poor?’ I just felt like that was a death sentence. That’s what outraged me and motivated me. When I came back, I was never the same.” She couldn’t just turn her back on these children and women. She had to do something.That something became a non-profit organisation called Keep a Child Alive. True to its name, its mission was to keep children alive. The aim was to support children facing the most challenging circumstances. Keys built the organisation with AIDS activist Leigh Blake, who had already worked on the issue for years. Blake had helped organise a 2001 remake of Marvin Gaye’s “What’s Going On” to raise AIDS awareness, with Bono as co-executive producer, and had funded a clinic in Kenya. Keep a Child Alive launched in 2003 with a simple aim: to get life-saving AIDS medication to children and families who could not afford it. Blake took the lead on the medical and fundraising side, while Keys became the public face. Keys’ contribution over the years has been steady. Its annual fundraiser, the Black Ball, has been a regular fixture on New York’s calendar.The non-profit has 41 partners, according to the organisation. The Hell’s Kitchen partnership was one of the group’s more visible recent efforts. Starting in April 2024, the production and ticketing partner TodayTix Group pledged $1 from every ticket sold for the Broadway run. In October, the show announced that it had donated $1 million, including matching gifts. The charity said that sum would reach 18,250 children across eight countries. A later statement put the total at more than $1.5 million.“I have taken such pride in being a co-founder of Keep a Child Alive since its creation over 20 years ago and all the lives we have been able to touch and all that we have been able to accomplish so far. Hell's Kitchen is about a 17-year-old girl trying to find her way in NYC. Both Hell's Kitchen and Keep a Child Alive believe that every child in the world should have the opportunity to thrive. I feel immense gratitude that we can partner, with equal passion, to create an even greater force for change,” Alicia Keys said in a statement released on the non-profit’s website.Keys started the organisation to get antiretroviral drugs to children who had no other route to treatment. It was an emergency effort to reach families in South Africa, Uganda, India, Kenya and Rwanda. Over time, the mission widened to cover health, education and human rights, though HIV remains at its centre.
Article Summary: Alicia Keys was just 20 when she travelled to South Africa as part of MTV’s Staying Alive campaign. She witnessed widows and children orphaned by AIDS struggling to survive. The experience inspired her to co-found Keep a Child Alive in 2003 with AIDS activist Leigh Blake.

Article Title: 74-year-old Florida man charged with murder offers to plead guilty for a Philly cheesesteak, fries and Pepsi, saying he'll accept life in prison; judge rejects his bizarre deal
Article Text:
Florida man specifies his demands for a guilty plea

Why the judge rejected the offer

Who is Robert Kessler?

What happened to Stephanie Crone-Overholt?

Evidence cited by investigators

Kessler changes his mind about representing himself

A 74-year-old Florida man facing a first-degree murder charge offered to plead guilty and accept a life sentence if a judge agreed to give him a Philly cheesesteak, fries and a Pepsi. Robert Kessler made the unusual proposal on October 26, 2026, during jury selection in his trial over the 2021 death of 47-year-old Stephanie Crone-Overholt. He also argued that accepting the deal would save taxpayers the expense of a trial. However, Hillsborough Circuit Judge Nick Nazaretian rejected the request, explaining that he could not provide food as an incentive for a guilty plea. Kessler subsequently withdrew his offer and asked the court to proceed with jury selection. He faces charges of first-degree murder and abuse of a dead body.Kessler made the offer after Judge Nazaretian explained that he could enter an open guilty plea, potentially receive a life sentence and bring the case to an end without a trial.In response, Kessler told the court he would accept the arrangement in exchange for a Philly cheesesteak, an order of fries and a Pepsi.When the judge asked him to clarify his request, Kessler specified that he wanted onions and mayonnaise on his sandwich, along with fries and a 20-ounce soft drink.He argued that the arrangement would benefit taxpayers by avoiding the cost of a lengthy criminal trial. However, the judge made it clear that a guilty plea could not be exchanged for a meal.“I can't obviously give food to people to enter a plea,” Nazaretian said, describing the proposed arrangement as inappropriate.The judge offered to ensure that Kessler received lunch that day but did not promise him the specific meal he had requested.The judge's response meant that Kessler could not secure the proposed arrangement. A guilty plea must be entered through the proper legal process, rather than in exchange for a personal reward from the court.After the judge rejected his request, Kessler indicated that he did not want to proceed with the proposed plea and asked for jury selection to continue.He suggested that he might have considered pleading guilty if he had received the sandwich, but acknowledged that the judge was unlikely to agree.Consequently, the exchange did not result in a guilty plea, and the criminal proceedings continued.Kessler is accused of killing Stephanie Crone-Overholt, a 47-year-old woman originally from Pennsylvania, and disposing of her dismembered remains in McKay Bay near Tampa.He faces charges of first-degree murder and abuse of a dead body. If convicted of first-degree murder, he faces a mandatory life sentence, according to reports on the case.Kessler has been in custody since 2021 and has been awaiting trial for nearly five years. He initially chose to represent himself despite having no formal legal training and facing significant challenges because of his visual impairment.The judge repeatedly warned him about the risks of defending himself in a serious criminal case. His decision to represent himself became a major issue during the proceedings.Crone-Overholt's dismembered remains were discovered by fishermen in McKay Bay in November 2021, prompting a criminal investigation.According to allegations outlined in an investigative affidavit, she had been staying at a home shared by Kessler and his daughter shortly before she disappeared.The affidavit also described an alleged argument between Kessler and Crone-Overholt. Kessler's daughter reportedly told investigators that Crone-Overholt had asked for $200 so she could leave.Investigators allege that Kessler killed the woman and disposed of her remains in the bay. He has been charged in connection with her death, but the allegations must be established through the criminal proceedings.The prosecution's case includes witness accounts and forensic evidence gathered during the investigation.According to reports describing the affidavit, at least three witnesses told investigators they had seen a man matching Kessler's description throwing bags into the bay around the time of Crone-Overholt's disappearance.Investigators also reportedly found blood evidence in Kessler's home and vehicles that testing linked to Crone-Overholt.The prosecution is expected to rely on such evidence as it presents its case. The defence has challenged aspects of the evidence, including a witness identification.Kessler's guilt or innocence will ultimately be determined through the legal process. He remains accused of the offences and is presumed innocent unless convicted.The cheesesteak proposal was not the only unusual development during the trial proceedings.Kessler initially insisted on representing himself, declining the assistance of his public defender despite warnings about the difficulties of handling a murder trial without legal training.His eyesight also presented practical challenges. During earlier proceedings, he described his vision as severely limited, saying he could barely distinguish objects. The court discussed ways to help him access documents and participate in his defence.On October 27, Kessler changed his position and indicated that he no longer wanted to represent himself, turning again to his public defender. He also told the judge that he preferred not to remain physically present in the courtroom during the trial.Nazaretian warned that being absent could disadvantage his defence, as Kessler might miss testimony or lose opportunities to alert his lawyer to information relevant to the case. The judge said jurors would be instructed not to interpret his absence as evidence of guilt or innocence.The proceedings continued as the court addressed these issues and moved forward with the murder trial.
Article Summary: Robert Kessler, 74, is accused of killing Stephanie Crone-Overholt, 47, and disposing of her dismembered remains in McKay Bay near Tampa. He faces charges of first-degree murder and abuse of a dead body. He initially chose to represent himself despite having no formal legal training and facing significant challenges because of his visual impairment. On October 27, he changed his mind about representing himself.

Article Title: In 2019, a Montana rancher found a rare dinosaur skeleton on her land; seven years later, the 70%-complete Nanotyrannus sold for $47.3 million at a New York auction, far above its $9 million top estim
Article Text:
Rising fossil prices are raising concerns that wealthy collectors could take rare specimens away from scientific research.

From Montana ranch to Manhattan auction

A smaller, sleeker tyrannosaur

A fossil with a remarkable neighbourhood

Twelve minutes, millions of dollars

The debate beyond the auction room

For decades, the Nanotyrannus occupied an uncertain place in the dinosaur world, caught between scientific classification and the shadow of its much more famous relative, Tyrannosaurus rex. Now, a remarkably preserved skeleton has given the disputed dinosaur a new kind of distinction: becoming one of the most valuable dinosaur fossils ever sold.Known as Jodi, the nearly 70%-complete skeleton fetched $47.3 million at a Sotheby’s auction in New York, dramatically surpassing its top estimate of $9 million. The sale, reported by The Associated Press, makes Jodi the second-most expensive dinosaur fossil ever sold, narrowly behind the $50.1 million record set by a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton called Gus earlier this year.Jodi’s journey began in 2019, when Montana rancher Jodi Pierson discovered the fossil on her property in the Hell Creek Formation, one of North America’s richest and most extensively studied dinosaur sites. The specimen was subsequently excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.According to BBC, the skeleton was initially presented as a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex. That classification reflected a debate that had persisted for decades: whether Nanotyrannus was genuinely a separate dinosaur or simply a younger form of T.rex.Research published last year helped settle the question in favour of Nanotyrannus being a distinct genus. The finding dramatically changed the significance of specimens such as Jodi, placing them among an extremely limited group of known Nanotyrannus skeletons.Jodi is one of only three relatively complete examples known to science. The mounted skeleton stands about 9 feet 6 inches tall and stretches nearly 20 feet from snout to tail.Although Nanotyrannus lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex approximately 67 million years ago, it was considerably smaller. Jodi is roughly half the length of an adult T. rex, while its anatomy gives it a distinctly different appearance.The dinosaur had relatively longer forelimbs, larger hand claws and narrower, blade-like teeth. Its lighter, more slender build has helped distinguish it from the bulkier T. rex.According to CNN, Jodi consists of 191 fossil-bone elements and includes an exceptionally well-preserved skull. The specimen is considered an adult based on its size and bone development. Missing portions have been supplemented with custom 3D-printed and sculpted elements, allowing the skeleton to be displayed in a complete mounted form.Its rarity appears to have been central to the extraordinary auction result. With only a handful of known Nanotyrannus skeletons, the specimen offered collectors an opportunity to own an unusually complete example of a dinosaur whose scientific identity itself was only recently clarified.Jodi was not the only extraordinary discovery to emerge from the Hell Creek Formation. The same region has produced some of the most important Tyrannosaurus rex fossils ever found.Phipps also discovered the celebrated Dueling Dinosaurs in 2006, roughly eight miles from where Jodi was found. The fossil preserves the remains of a Triceratops and a smaller tyrannosaur apparently locked together, and it later became important to research supporting Nanotyrannus as a distinct genus.Another known Nanotyrannus skeleton, Jane, is housed at the Burpee Museum of Natural History in Illinois.The history of the region therefore adds another layer to Jodi’s importance. What began as a discovery on a working Montana ranch became part of a much larger scientific story about the diversity of tyrannosaurs during the Late Cretaceous period.At Sotheby’s, six prospective buyers competed for Jodi during a roughly 12-minute auction. The winning bidder, who participated online or by phone, has chosen to remain anonymous.The final price was more than five times the auction house’s lower estimate and substantially exceeded its $6 million to $9 million expected range. The result placed Jodi just behind Gus in the hierarchy of dinosaur fossil sales. The Stegosaurus known as Apex, which sold for $44.6 million in 2024, now ranks third, states BBC report.The price also highlights the extraordinary market that has developed around scientifically significant fossils, particularly exceptionally preserved dinosaur skeletons, adds CNN.Jodi’s sale has also revived a long-running debate over who should own important fossils and where they should ultimately be kept.Scientists have expressed concern that privately owned specimens can disappear from public view, limiting opportunities for researchers to study them and preventing museums, students and visitors from accessing them.BBC reported that palaeontologists have warned that increasingly high auction prices could encourage a new era of fossil collecting among ultra-wealthy buyers. The concern is particularly acute for rare specimens whose scientific importance may not yet be fully understood.At the same time, the debate is not entirely one-sided. The excavation of large fossils can require considerable expertise, labour, equipment and financial investment, particularly when specimens are located on privately owned land.For now, Jodi’s future remains uncertain. Its anonymous new owner has acquired a fossil that is not only exceptionally rare but also scientifically significant at a moment when Nanotyrannus has finally emerged from decades of classification controversy.Whether Jodi becomes part of a public exhibition or disappears into a private collection, its extraordinary sale has ensured that this once-mysterious dinosaur will remain at the centre of the palaeontology conversation.Images Courtesy: Reuters
Article Summary: The nearly 70%-complete skeleton fetched $47.3 million at a Sotheby’s auction in New York, dramatically surpassing its top estimate of $9 million. The sale makes Jodi the second-most expensive dinosaur fossil ever sold, narrowly behind the $50.1 million record set by a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton called Gus.

Article Title: Maryland removed its Cypress Mill dam in 2025; officials report more than 35 miles of fish habitat reopened, while early plans estimated 18 miles
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing an ageing mill dam with a broad pond behind its concrete spillway, illustrating the type of barrier removed to reopen fish habitat in Maryland. Credits - Gemini

A dam from the mill era

Taking it down

AI-generated representative image showing a restored freshwater channel with flowing water and stabilised natural banks, illustrating the habitat reconnection achieved through dam removal. Credits - Gemini

What the river gets back

Dams built to power mills can continue to obstruct migratory fish long after their original purpose has ended. One such structure stood near Millington on Maryland's Eastern Shore, where Cypress Branch Dam was removed in 2025 after decades of deterioration and planning.
