Although the dam had breached years earlier, the remaining structure continued to impede fish passage.The structure, called Cypress Branch Dam in state records and also known as Cypress Mill Dam, was built to hold water for the mill races in Millington. Its exact construction date is unknown, but consultants estimated that it dated to about 1900 based on the aggregate in the concrete. The Maryland Department of Natural Resources reports that removal was completed in April 2025, reopening more than 35 miles of habitat for herring, hickory shad and other fish. The project required years of planning, several rounds of funding and work to resolve a railway crossing issue.The dam consisted of an earthen berm and a concrete spillway. It had breached decades before its removal and was in an advanced state of disrepair, but the remaining structure still obstructed fish passage. A large mill pond to the north fed a smaller pond to the south, which supplied the mill races in Millington.No one knows exactly when it was built. The state’s history of the site says there have been dams and mill ponds in the area since the 18th century. Consultants from Hurt and Proffitt estimated the current dam dated to about 1900, based on the aggregate in the concrete. The estate passed through a lengthy line of owners, including Philadelphia merchant Thomas Gilpin in the 1760s and subsequently the Higman family, whose grist mill gave the property one of its names. The mill pond property was purchased by the state of Maryland in 1994. It is currently part of Cypress Branch State Park.American Rivers, which worked with the state on the restoration, said the history is a remnant of the Eastern Shore’s milling era with no recognised builder. Work started in 2019 when the Maryland Geological Survey tested the silt behind the dam and discovered it wasn’t toxic and the amounts were low because the dam had been ruptured for so long, American Rivers said.The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service was an early booster, seeing an opportunity to reunite more than 35 miles of habitat. Then the pandemic slowed the design work. Construction expenses went up. And the project required more money. That came in the form of a grant from the Environmental Protection Agency, through the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. Permits took time, too, in part because the site needed historical mitigation and a strategy for what to do if the restoration didn’t work out the way they hoped.Construction began in early 2025. Crews demolished the concrete of the old spillway, relocated parts of the earthen dam and straightened out a canal that had broken up into multiple pieces to go around the spillway. They also built big structures of root wad along the banks to hold the soil in place. A late issue was a railway crossing near the access road, which was rectified on the way out thanks to a state financial increase.The target species include alewife and blueback herring, collectively known as river herring, and hickory shad. These fish spend their adult lives in the Atlantic and return to freshwater each spring to spawn. An early Maryland Department of Natural Resources planning document estimated that the project would reconnect 18 miles of habitat, comprising more than eight miles of Cypress Branch and 10 miles of tributaries. After completion, the department reported that the project reopened more than 35 miles of habitat. The two figures come from different stages of the project, and the published documents do not explain exactly how the latter total was calculated.The project forms part of a wider effort to restore migratory fish routes throughout the Chesapeake Bay watershed. The Chesapeake Bay Program originally set a goal of opening 1,000 additional stream miles to fish passage by 2025. Partners achieved that target in 2016, nine years ahead of schedule. Under a later goal, partners opened 303 stream miles during 2022 and 2023. These are separate milestones, so the later figures do not conflict with the earlier achievement. The Cypress Branch project team also established a monitoring plan to assess whether herring and shad return in healthy numbers. After the restoration work, American Rivers documented an osprey catching a fish in the former pond area. The Cypress Branch project shows that a breached, disused dam can continue to impede fish migration long after its original purpose has disappeared. Its removal restored access to upstream habitat, and monitoring will help determine how herring and shad use the connected streams.
Article Summary: Cypress Branch Dam was built to hold water for the mill races in Millington, Maryland. It had breached years earlier, but the remaining structure continued to impede fish passage. The project required years of planning, several rounds of funding and work to resolve a railway crossing issue. The Maryland Department of Natural Resources reports that removal was completed in April 2025.

Article Title: In New Hampshire, Bob and Ruth Morrell turned more than 25 German storybook dolls into a village in 1954; Story Land now has more than 50 attractions
Article Text:
Cinderella's Castle, the centrepiece of Story Land theme park in Glen, New Hampshire. Credits - Wikipedia

A knock at the door

Early years of risk

Roar-O-Saurus's lift hill and first drop, with the coaster's Triceratops-themed train going down the latter. Credits - Wikipedia

A park that kept growing

Story Land in Glen, New Hampshire, grew from a collection of handmade storybook dolls into a theme park for young families. Its founders, Bob and Ruth Morrell, opened the park in late 1954 after dollmaker Frau Edith Von Arps suggested building a village around the figures. The Morrells expanded her idea to include storybook characters, rides and play areas. Story Land’s official history recounts how the idea developed. The park opened with a single ride, a fire engine that Bob drove with children as passengers. Over the decades, it added attractions such as Cinderella’s Pumpkin Coach and Castle in 1957 and continued expanding. Story Land now advertises more than 50 attractions, including rides, shows and play areas.Bob Morrell had been in the 10th Mountain Division of ski soldiers in the Second World War and had been recalled to service during the Korean Conflict. That took the pair to Germany, when an elderly woman named Frau Edith Von Arps showed up at their home. She was travelling from home to house selling dolls she had handcrafted, one for each classic children’s fairy tale.The Morrells became friends with Von Arps, who sold them more than 25 dolls before they returned to New Hampshire.She suggested that they build a small village around the dolls. The Morrells expanded the idea beyond a display, planning rides and play spaces where storybook creatures could live and characters could come to life.This was not their first rodeo in business. They owned the Eastern Slope Ice Cream Company in North Conway, the Concord Monitor reported. The park began with around $5,000, the New Hampshire Union Leader reported. They purchased a piece of land in Glen that the previous owner said wouldn’t even make a respectable pasture.The park opened in late 1954, a year before Disneyland came up and transformed people’s expectations of amusement parks. According to the Conway Daily Sun, it was once called Story Town and had only one ride, a fire engine Bob drove with youngsters as passengers. Then came a few successful seasons, aided by the arrival of Cinderella’s Pumpkin Coach and Castle in 1957. Then the national economy stalled, and the fledgling park struggled. The local lenders didn’t want the mortgage on the home of the three bears, and the family got by working hard and giving money back into the park year after year. That habit paid off in the late 1960s. Bob bought an old German carousel in 1967 that still turns today, a train and a fleet of boats that became the Swan Boats. The Morrells had room to dream bigger, and visitors began to perceive the park as a location they wanted to return to.The 1970s were a busy decade. New additions included a chapel, a safari ride, a Moroccan bazaar, the first maze, a Dutch village with a shoe ride and a coaster that later became the Polar Coaster. The 1980s brought a pirate ship, a tea cup ride and a trip to the moon. The park’s latest new ride was a compact wooden coaster with a 40-foot drop, which opened in 2014. Its more recent major addition was Moo Lagoon, a water play area that debuted in 2024.The park continued as a family business through all this. Ruth handled the gift shop, Bob ran around making sure everyone was having fun, and their daughter Nancy played Mistress Mary in her garden as a child. Their son Stoney continued the work until he died in 2006, and the Morrell family ran the park until 2007, the Concord Monitor reported. Story Land continues to combine storybook settings with rides, shows and play areas for young visitors. The park’s official media information lists more than 50 attractions and describes its history of entertaining generations of families since opening in 1954.
Article Summary: Story Land in Glen, New Hampshire, opened in late 1954. Its founders, Bob and Ruth Morrell, bought a piece of land that the previous owner said wouldn’t even make a respectable pasture. The park opened with a single ride, a fire engine Bob drove with children as passengers. Over the decades, it added attractions such as Cinderella’s Pumpkin Coach and Castle in 1957 and continued expanding.

Article Title: From 1997 to 2002, wildlife officials released 1,550 elk in southeastern Kentucky; the herd has since grown to more than 10,000 across a 16-county restoration zone
Article Text:
An elk in a forest. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Bringing native species back to Kentucky

A 16-county zone with varied elk distribution

A couple of elk in nature. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

From restoration to long-term population management

Between December 1997 and March 2002, wildlife authorities released approximately 1,550 elk in southeastern Kentucky. This release began a restoration programme that has since established one of the largest elk herds in the eastern United States. The animals were captured in six western states and transported to Kentucky, where elk had disappeared during the 19th century. According to the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources (KDFWR), the state now has an estimated population of more than 10,000 elk. The animals reportedly occupy a designated restoration zone covering 16 counties and around 4.1 million acres.Historical data indicate that elk once roamed the state, but habitat degradation and overhunting eliminated its population by the mid-1880s. Wildlife officials and conservation advocates were looking into ways to restore the species to its historical range by the late 20th century. In 1997, the KDFWR conducted a habitat feasibility study and set up public meetings to assess whether southeastern Kentucky could support a free-ranging herd. The agency identified suitable land and found substantial public support for the idea, thus allowing the restoration initiative to proceed.The department obtained elk from six western states: Arizona, Kansas, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oregon and Utah. In December 1997, the captures began, and the animals underwent disease testing before being transported to Kentucky. Releases took place through March 2002, with Harlan, Knott, Leslie, Letcher, Martin, Perry and Pike counties being the initial release sites.The state’s elk management zone encompasses approximately 4.1 million acres across 16 counties in the southeastern part of the state. The original zone included 14 counties, with Whitley and McCreary counties added in 2004 to provide a travel corridor between Kentucky’s restoration zone and Tennessee’s elk restoration area. The landscape includes deciduous forests, active and reclaimed surface mines, agricultural or cleared land, and smaller areas for urban development.However, elk numbers are not distributed evenly across all 16 counties. KDFWR's report suggests that many animals remain concentrated around the original release sites, while some peripheral areas have lower densities or few elk. The department has now undertaken additional translocations within the state, moving animals from areas with established populations to locations where their presence remains limited, to address this uneven distribution challenge.In the winter of December 2022, one important step occurred when wildlife officials relocated 43 elk from neighbouring counties to McCreary County. The operation helped establish a new population in an area of the county that had suitable habitat but lacked a resident herd. KDFWR described the move as the final step in its restoration activities, while noting that the programme continues to manage elk distribution and population levels.As the herd became established, Kentucky introduced regulated hunting as part of its management programme. The first modern hunt of the state took place in 2001, when 12 permits were issued, and six bulls and six cows were harvested. Subsequently, the number of permits changed as officials adjusted hunting opportunities and management objectives. In 2024, the department reportedly made 500 elk permits available.The state’s wildlife department estimates the current population at more than 10,000 elk using two models: a life-table model and statistical population reconstruction. These methods draw on data used by wildlife managers to estimate abundance; however, the resulting figure is not a direct count of every animal across the state. The programme has therefore moved past its original task of returning elk to Kentucky. Wildlife managers now focus on maintaining the herd, managing its distribution, monitoring population trends and balancing habitat needs with opportunities for hunting and wildlife viewing.
Article Summary: Kentucky has one of the largest elk herds in the eastern United States. The state now has an estimated population of more than 10,000 elk. The animals occupy a designated restoration zone covering 16 counties and around 4.1 million acres. But elk numbers are not distributed evenly across all 16 counties.

Article Title: A Virginia family’s land held a 200-year-old dam once used by a five-story grain mill; removal reopened 30 miles of stream, and mussel beds began returning
Article Text:
AI Representation: Virginia’s Little River Mill Dam, built between 1818 and 1834 to serve a five-story grain mill, was removed in 2024. Image credits: Chatgpt

A dam and five-story mill built between 1818 and 1834 on the Bowen family’s land

A river system with 46 mussel species, 20 of them endangered

A $200,000 grant, a notching phase and more than 30 miles of stream

Dam for the Versailles Mill. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A 2007 USGS report on host fish and mussels in the Neversink River

Relations of Environmental Factors with Mussel-Species Richness in the Neversink River, New York

A four-year study of small dam removal on North Carolina’s Deep River

Short-term effects of small dam removal on freshwater mussel assemblage

Old mill dams are easy to overlook on farmland. Often, they linger on private property long after the mill they were built for is gone. The people who live near them may never consider their effect on the river. In southwest Virginia, there was such a dam on one family’s farm. The mill it once powered had been long gone, but the dam and its effect on the river system remained.The US Fish and Wildlife Service reported that the Bowen family has been tied to its land at Maiden Spring, Virginia, for about 250 years, or seven generations by the Service’s count. The ancestors first inhabited the area during the 1760s near a spring that feeds a creek into the Little River, which is a major tributary of the Clinch River. The Little River was dammed somewhere between 1818 and 1834, with a five-story mill being erected to process the grains produced at the settlement. The mill was later torn down, but the dam, 130 feet wide and 14 feet tall, survived. The family had long been good stewards of the land, planting native trees near the water and fencing cattle out of the river. However, the three Bowen brothers, who currently operate the family farm, were unaware of the fact that the disused dam was hindering certain fish and mussel species.The Service describes the Clinch River system as one of the most ecologically valuable and diverse freshwater areas in North America, home to 100 fish species, five of them threatened or endangered and 46 freshwater mussel species, 20 of them endangered. The river also hosts the largest concentration of federally protected species in the United States. Corey Kanuckel, a Service biologist with the Partners for Fish and Wildlife office in Virginia, approached the brothers about the dam. Surveys found no mussels above the dam in the channel or within 200 meters of its base. Kanuckel named several species affected by the dam: the Cumberland moccasinshell and Tennessee clubshell, both at-risk species, the listed slabside pearlymussel and the Tennessee pigtoe, which the Service’s 2024 story says is proposed for the endangered species list.The brothers accepted removal in exchange for a promise from the Service to restore the property in a better state and an added benefit that removal would reduce a hazard and liability. Gravel was provided by the Service to make sure that heavily used sections of the land were stabilized, allowing farm lanes to remain accessible. The US Fish and Wildlife Service awarded the Canaan Valley Institute $200,000 through the National Fish Passage Program, which received funding under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, for the Little River Dam removal project, according to the Service’s April 2024 story.Notches were first cut into the dam to allow passage of water without bringing too much sediment, followed by the removal of the remaining dam and restoration of the streambank. The Service’s April 2024 story said the removal was complete and had opened 30 miles of stream, with bank stabilization under way and due to finish in summer 2024. The Service also reported promising mussel bed development downstream. Its project page is less consistent on mileage: the summary says over 30 miles, while the Quick Facts table lists 50 stream miles reconnected. The page does not explain the difference., describes a 6-year study of seven mussel species. It notes that mussel larvae develop in species-specific host fish, so impoundments that block those fish also limit where mussels can live. Removing the Cuddebackville Dam gave diadromous and other fish that host rare mussels access to habitat they could not reach before. From 1997 to 2002, the team sampled 28 sites across the river and its tributaries, then built a model linking mussel richness to 10 environmental variables, including elevation, drainage area, channel width, sand content, velocity, shear stress, ANC and calcium, phosphorus and sulfate concentrations. The endangered dwarf wedgemussel and threatened swollen wedgemussel occurred alongside five other species.A 2013 paper in Walkerana , tracked mussels for four years after a small hydropower dam came out of North Carolina’s Deep River in 2006. Its before-after-control-impact analyses showed no significant change in mussel density or species richness at the tailrace or the drained impoundment and stranding in the dewatered reservoir caused little mortality. The authors monitored two impact sites and two reference sites each year, using transect surveys and quadrat excavation to track density, richness and survival. Apparent annual survival of Eastern Elliptio at the tailrace did not differ from control sites. They concluded that careful planning, timing and method can limit short-term harm. Neither study looked at the Little River, but together they show why removing a dam matters for mussels and what removal can do to the mussels already living below it. The Service says the mussel beds downstream are still in an early stage of recovery.
Article Summary: Virginia’s Little River Mill Dam, built between 1818 and 1834 to serve a five- story grain mill, was removed in 2024. The Bowen family has been tied to its land at Maiden Spring, Virginia, for about 250 years. The family had long been good stewards of the land, planting native trees near the water and fencing cattle out of the river.

Article Title: Lauren Sánchez Bezos-backed fund commits $4.8 million to 48 climate solutions that missed Earthshot Prize finals; funding supports projects ranging from carbon removal to wildlife protection
Article Text:
Bezos Earth Fund commits $4.8 million to climate and nature solutions

The first 16 organisations selected for funding

1. Air Protein, Inc.

2. Climatenza Solar

3. Instituto Floresta Viva

4. Forum Konservasi Leuser

5. Fundación Rewilding Argentina

6. Hyperion Robotics

7. InPlanet

8. Lasso

9. Mandai Nature

10. Mati Carbon

11. MERMAID

12. Asociación Conservacionista Misión Tiburón

13. Simple Planet

14. Snowchange Cooperative

15. tHEMEat Company

16. UP Catalyst

The significance of the Earthshot Prize partnership

The Bezos Earth Fund's wider environmental mission

The Bezos Earth Fund, chaired by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, with Lauren Sanchez Bezos serving as vice chair, has committed $4.8 million over three years to support 48 climate and nature solutions nominated for the Earthshot Prize but not selected as finalists. Announced on February 4, 2026, the initiative is a collaboration between the Bezos Earth Fund and the Earthshot Prize to help promising environmental projects expand their operations and increase their impact. The programme will support 16 organisations each year, with each organisation in the first cohort receiving $100,000. The selected organisations work across areas including carbon removal, wildlife conservation, ecosystem restoration and sustainable technology. The initiative aims to extend funding opportunities beyond the prize's annual finalists and winners.The three-year partnership will draw from the Earthshot Prize's global pool of nominees who did not make the final shortlist. The Bezos Earth Fund will provide $4.8 million in total, supporting 16 organisations annually with grants of $100,000 each.The funding is intended to help selected organisations scale their work and reach more communities, ecosystems and industries.The initiative brings together the Earthshot Prize's international network of environmental innovators and the Bezos Earth Fund's philanthropic resources to help promising solutions progress beyond their existing scale.Dr Kelly Levin, chief of science, data and systems change at the Bezos Earth Fund, said promising innovations often remain small when the world needs them to expand. She said the partnership could help these ideas grow into solutions capable of delivering wider environmental benefits.Jason Knauf, chief executive of the Earthshot Prize, said the prize's wider nomination pool represents a global pipeline of environmental innovators and potential solutions. The collaboration will allow the organisations to support additional projects beyond the prize's annual selection process.The first cohort includes organisations working on carbon removal, cleaner industrial processes, wildlife protection, habitat restoration and other environmental challenges. Each will receive $100,000 to help expand its operations and amplify its impact.Air Protein develops alternative proteins using microorganisms and processes that use carbon dioxide as a feedstock. Its approach explores ways to produce protein without relying entirely on conventional agriculture and livestock farming.Climatenza Solar is among the first cohort of selected organisations. Its inclusion places it within the initiative's wider effort to support climate-focused innovation, although the announcement does not specify the particular solar technology or project the grant will support.Instituto Floresta Viva is a Brazilian environmental organisation associated with Atlantic Forest conservation and restoration. Its work provides a nature-restoration angle within a programme designed to help environmental solutions expand.Forum Konservasi Leuser works on protecting the Leuser Ecosystem in Indonesia, an important rainforest landscape in Sumatra that provides habitat for threatened wildlife. Its conservation work is linked to safeguarding forests and biodiversity.The Argentine conservation organisation works to protect and restore ecosystems, recover native wildlife and establish protected areas. Its projects include rewilding initiatives and efforts to reconnect habitats while supporting local economies linked to nature.Hyperion Robotics develops robotic construction technology designed to reduce waste and the carbon footprint of infrastructure. Its approach focuses on improving how concrete foundations are designed and built, including for energy and industrial infrastructure.InPlanet works on enhanced rock weathering, a carbon-removal approach that involves spreading finely crushed silicate rock on agricultural land to accelerate natural chemical reactions that remove carbon dioxide. The process can also improve soil conditions by releasing minerals and helping correct soil acidity.Lasso is associated with technology for recovering and recycling materials, including plastics. Its work offers a potential route to reducing waste and recovering resources that would otherwise be discarded.Based in Singapore, Mandai Nature supports wildlife conservation and ecosystem protection, particularly in Southeast Asia. It works with local organisations and other partners to protect threatened species, restore habitats and support communities involved in conservation.Mati Carbon uses enhanced rock weathering to remove carbon dioxide while working with farmers. Its approach involves spreading natural rock dust on agricultural land, where it can help improve soil conditions and support durable carbon removal.MERMAID operates a digital platform that helps scientists and conservation practitioners collect, manage and share coral reef monitoring data. The information can support research and decisions about reef conservation and management.This Costa Rican conservation organisation focuses on marine life, including shark conservation. Its work is associated with protecting threatened marine species and promoting the conservation of ocean ecosystems.Simple Planet is among the selected organisations working within the climate and nature innovation landscape. The funding announcement does not specify the precise solution or project for which it will use the grant.Snowchange Cooperative works with Indigenous peoples and local communities on ecological restoration, biodiversity protection and the preservation of traditional knowledge. Its work includes community-led efforts to protect and restore northern ecosystems.tHEMEat Company is included in the first cohort of environmental innovators. Its specific grant-funded activities are not detailed in the announcement, so the precise technology or solution being supported remains to be established from further project information.UP Catalyst develops technologies that use captured carbon dioxide to produce carbon materials, including graphite and carbon nanotubes. Its approach explores ways to turn carbon into useful industrial materials rather than allowing it to remain in the atmosphere.The first cohort spans different approaches to environmental challenges, from carbon removal and alternative proteins to conservation and construction technology. The $100,000 grants are intended to help each selected organisation expand its work, although the announcement does not provide individual spending plans or quantified impact targets for all 16 recipients.Founded by Prince William in 2020, the Earthshot Prize aims to identify and scale solutions to five major environmental challenges: protecting and restoring nature, cleaning the air, reviving the oceans, building a waste-free world and fixing the climate.The prize selects 15 finalists each year, with five winners receiving £1 million each. Its wider nomination pool, however, includes many other organisations working on environmental problems that do not reach the final stage.The Bezos Earth Fund partnership creates an additional funding route for selected nominees outside the finalist group. Rather than concentrating support only on the annual finalists and winners, the initiative aims to help other promising projects develop and expand their reach.The collaboration reflects the view that environmental innovation can emerge from a wide range of sources, including research organisations, technology developers, conservation groups and local communities. Providing additional funding may help selected projects move beyond their current scale and reach more people or ecosystems.Jeff Bezos announced the creation of the Bezos Earth Fund in 2020, committing $10 billion to efforts addressing climate change and protecting nature. The fund supports work with organisations around the world on environmental protection, restoration and the development of climate solutions.The partnership with the Earthshot Prize forms part of this broader philanthropic effort. By supporting selected nominees who did not become finalists, the initiative seeks to expand the pool of environmental innovators receiving financial support.The programme will run over three years, with 16 organisations selected annually. Its overall objective is to help promising climate and nature solutions grow beyond their existing operations and contribute to wider environmental progress.
Article Summary: The Bezos Earth Fund has committed $4.8 million over three years to support 48 climate and nature solutions nominated for the Earthshot Prize but not selected as finalists. The programme will support 16 organisations each year, with each organisation in the first cohort receiving $100,000. The initiative aims to extend funding opportunities beyond the prize's annual finalists and winners.

Article Title: Idaho’s 3-foot dam, built in the 1930s, powered one ranger station; removed in 2021, it reopened five miles of spawning habitat for threatened bull trout
Article Text:
AI Representation: Idaho’s Red Ives Creek Dam, built in 1935 to provide hydroelectric power to the Red Ives Ranger Station, was removed in August 2021. Image credits: Chatgpt

A roughly 3- to 5-foot-tall and 25-foot-wide dam on

Red Ives Creek

Removal in August 2021 and a project cost of $127,693

Five miles of habitat for threatened bull trout in the St. Joe River headwaters

The St. Joe River at Red Ives in Idaho’s Panhandle, where the removal of a small obsolete dam reopened access to upstream trout habitat. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Large dams draw most of the attention in discussions about fish and rivers, but small, old structures matter too. Most of them stay in western rivers long after their usefulness has passed. Even a structure a few feet high is enough to alter the way water flows and the movement of fish. In northern Idaho, one such dam sat low in a creek in a national forest. It had been built to provide power for a remote Forest Service ranger station. It remained long after it was useful and affected fish that most visitors never noticed.Sources differ on the dam’s size and age. The Open Rivers Fund lists it as 3 feet tall and built in 1930, while American Rivers gives 5 feet and 1935, a date the Restoration Partnership also uses and both put its width at about 25 feet. It was a small concrete structure on Red Ives Creek, owned by the U.S. Forest Service, that supplied power to the Red Ives Ranger Station. That project page adds that the Civilian Conservation Corps built it and the Forest Service abandoned it in 1960, though Trout Unlimited Idaho says it powered the station into the mid 1980s. The dam restricted flows and increased water velocities, which reduced fish passage through the year and disrupted the movement of wood and gravel, the Open Rivers Fund notes.The fund also identified a hidden open shaft beside the dam, two feet wide and four feet deep.Trout Unlimited and the U.S. Forest Service removed the Red Ives Creek Dam in August 2021. The project cost $127,693, according to the Open Rivers Fund’s project page. The removal followed 20 years of waiting, American Rivers said. The structure held much more concrete and rebar than the partnership had expected, Trout Unlimited Idaho reported, but the job went quickly once the contractors started hammering. Nearly 60 cubic yards of concrete and steel were removed, the Restoration Partnership’s project page reports. The crews restored the creek profile using boulders and gravel from behind the dam, stabilized about 200 feet of bank and put 15 logs into place for habitat. A separate, later phase upstream of the former dam placed about 1,400 logs along roughly a mile of Red Ives Creek, in work completed in 2023 and 2025, Trout Unlimited reported.Removal opened fish passage to five miles of habitat for bull trout and westslope cutthroat trout and the Restoration Partnership describes those miles as spawning and rearing habitat. Idaho Fish and Game prohibits harvest of bull trout and only catch-and-release fishing is permitted. Sandpoint Magazine notes that bull trout spawn in the fall, which matters because many small barriers pass fish at some flows but not others.The headwater tributaries of the St. Joe River hold the last remaining bull trout population in the Coeur d’Alene Core Area, which is why Red Ives Creek was selected for restoration, the Restoration Partnership explains. Critical habitat for bull trout was designated in 2005 and revised in 2010, Idaho’s species website says and American Rivers highlights the 2010 designation.
Article Summary: The Red Ives Creek Dam in northern Idaho was built in 1935. The Civilian Conservation Corps built it and the Forest Service abandoned it in 1960. The dam restricted flows and increased water velocities, which reduced fish passage through the year and disrupted the movement of wood and gravel.

Article Title: An Indiana couple paid a contractor with cheques and a Ford F-350 truck for home repairs, but he made roof trusses in his backyard; on October 26 a court made him personally liable for an $82,020 judg
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Couple hired contractor for house and garage repairs

Manufactured roof trusses were never delivered

Construction company ordered to pay more than $82,000

Appeals court says contractor can be held personally liable

A home renovation project can turn into a costly dispute when promised materials never arrive and the work fails to meet the contract. In Indiana, a couple who hired a contractor to repair a house and garage secured an $82,020 judgment against his construction company after a court found that it had breached the contract and made material and fraudulent misrepresentations. On October 26, 2026, an appeals court ruled that the contractor himself could also be held personally liable.According to the Indiana Court of Appeals’ memorandum decision in Robert Burgner, et al. v. Jeremy Swenson, et al., available on Justia , the contractor had accepted cheques and a Ford F-350 truck as part of the arrangement, but the promised manufactured roof trusses were never supplied as agreed. The appellate court reversed the lower court’s refusal to impose personal liability on Jeremy Swenson, concluding that he could not use his company as a shield against responsibility for fraudulent conduct in which he had personally participated.The dispute began in early 2022, when Robert Burgner contacted Swenson about repairs and improvements to a property on Harrison Street in Veedersburg, Indiana. The property included a house and a garage that had been unoccupied for several years. Swenson operated a construction business called SwenCrest, LLC, of which he was the sole member. He prepared a written estimate on the company’s letterhead, outlining the planned work and estimated material costs.The contract, signed in April 2022, quoted a total of $25,286.75, with labour costs listed as zero. The parties agreed that Burgner would transfer ownership of a 2005 Ford F-350 truck as payment for the work.The agreement specified the use of manufactured roof trusses. The couple also made additional payments by cheque to cover materials, including $9,000 in April 2022 and $6,000 in July that year. The money was intended to pay for trusses and other construction materials, including roofing supplies.By July 2022, Burgner discovered that the roof trusses had not been ordered. He and Swenson subsequently visited Ferguson Lumber, where Swenson placed an order for the materials, which were expected to arrive in November. However, the lumber supplier later cancelled the order. According to an employee of Ferguson Lumber, the cancellation occurred because Swenson had an unpaid account with the supplier.In September 2022, Swenson took possession of the Ford F-350, and Burgner transferred the vehicle’s title documents, assigning the truck to SwenCrest, LLC. The following month, the couple issued another cheque for $2,023.36 at Swenson’s direction, making it payable to him personally. Swenson later acknowledged that he deposited the cheque electronically and then cashed it at the couple’s bank. He repaid the amount about 30 days after Burgner raised the issue.In November, Burgner visited Swenson’s home to investigate the missing trusses. There, he discovered trusses being constructed in the contractor’s backyard for the couple’s project. Burgner rejected them because the contract specified manufactured trusses rather than the ones being made on-site. The couple also encountered delays in the remaining work. Swenson claimed that he had obtained a building permit, but records from the Town of Veedersburg showed that neither he nor his company had applied for one for the property.In June 2023, the couple terminated the contract and demanded repayment of $17,000 paid for materials that had not been ordered, along with $10,000 for damage caused by faulty workmanship. They subsequently filed a lawsuit against Swenson, his wife and the construction business, alleging breach of contract, fraud and other claims.During the proceedings, evidence raised questions about the company’s financial records and its handling of funds. Swenson acknowledged that some personal expenses had appeared in the company’s bank account. He also could definitively identify only about $500 in receipts as relating to the Burgners’ project. In July 2025, the trial court found that SwenCrest had breached the contract and made material and fraudulent misrepresentations. It awarded the couple damages, including amounts they had paid, costs for repairs and further work by another contractor, estimated future repair costs, attorney’s fees and filing fees.After trebling the damages, the court entered judgment against SwenCrest, Inc., for $82,020.08, plus costs. However, it declined to hold Swenson personally liable, finding that the circumstances did not justify piercing the corporate veil. The couple challenged that part of the decision.The Indiana Court of Appeals concluded that Swenson could be held personally liable for his own participation in the fraudulent conduct, even without piercing the corporate veil. The judges explained that corporate officers and members of limited liability companies are generally protected from responsibility for business debts. However, that protection does not prevent them from being held personally liable for wrongful conduct in which they directly participate.The court noted that Swenson was the sole member of the LLC and the person who dealt with the couple throughout the transaction. He accepted their payments, failed to purchase materials as promised, did not disclose the cancellation of the truss order and attempted to construct the trusses himself despite the contract’s specifications. The court therefore reversed the decision refusing to hold Swenson personally liable and remanded the case with instructions to enter judgment against both Swenson and SwenCrest, Inc.The ruling does not mean that business owners are automatically responsible for every company debt. Instead, it reinforces the distinction between liability arising from a company’s obligations and liability arising from an individual’s own fraudulent conduct. The October 26 decision was issued as a memorandum decision and is not binding precedent under Indiana Appellate Rule 65(D), although it may be cited for persuasive value.
Article Summary: Couple hired contractor for house and garage repairs. Contractor accepted cheques and a Ford F-350 truck as part of the arrangement. But promised manufactured roof trusses were never supplied as agreed. Indiana Court of Appeals found contractor breached the contract and made material and fraudulent misrepresentations.

Article Title: In 2012, MIT professor Anant Agarwal put an undergraduate circuits course online for free; nearly 155,000 people registered to learn from the class
Article Text:
Anant Agarwal taught MITx’s first course, 6.002x: Circuits and Electronics, which opened to nearly 155,000 online registrants in 2012. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

MITx

opens with one course on March 5, 2012

Planned for 2,000 sign-ups, nearly 155,000 registered from more than 160 countries

From 23,349 first problem set attempts to 7,157 certificates

A 2013 paper on edX’s first

MOOC

, written by six researchers

Studying Learning in the Worldwide Classroom: Research into edX’s First MOOC

A paper from the course team: designed to be content-identical to MIT’s sophomore course

An edX course page illustrates the online-learning platform that grew out of MITx; the image shows a later MITx course, not the original 6.002x interface. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The first course in a new online-learning initiative at a US university was a sophomore-level electrical engineering class on circuits and electronics, a subject that students on campus often find difficult. Unlike a recorded lecture, it offered weekly video lessons, graded homework, online laboratories, exams that counted toward a certificate and a discussion forum and anyone with an internet connection could sign up for free. The course was a prototype, built to test whether much of a campus course could be delivered to learners anywhere and its organizers expected far fewer participants than actually registered. It became both the starting point for a larger platform and a source of data on how people learn in an open online course. The sections below follow the course’s launch, its enrollment and completion numbers, and the research it produced.MIT unveiled the MITx platform in December 2011 with one course, 6.002x Circuits and Electronics, taught by Anant Agarwal, who later became edX CEO, Class Central recounts. 6.002x launched on March 5, 2012 and ran through June 8, about 14 weeks.Agarwal, in an MIT YouTube video, named his teaching colleagues as Gerry Sussman, Chris Terman, Piotr Mitros and Jacob White. According to Class Central, everyone who registered got free access to an embedded textbook, one of whose authors was Agarwal. In May 2012, Harvard joined the effort and MITx became edX.MIT’s March 5, 2012 news release said more than 90,000 people had signed up for the prototype course since registration opened in February, far above the original estimate of 2,000 students. Technology Review quoted Agarwal as saying that 10,000 sign-ups would be a fantastic success. Registration kept growing during the run and by the end almost 155,000 people from more than 160 countries had registered, according to the MIT News account that ACM carries. Agarwal compared that figure with the number of students he estimated might have taken the course at MIT over 40 years.The attrition shows what registering meant. Of the 154,763 students who registered, 23,349 tried the first problem set, 10,547 made it to the midterm, 9,318 passed it, 8,240 took the final and 7,157 earned a certificate, according to the 2013 paper discussed below. MIT News also reports that a 15-year-old student in Mongolia was one of 341 students to score full marks on the final exam. Access to the course was free, but the certificate process evolved over time. MIT announced on February 13, 2012, that students who mastered the prototype course would receive a certificate free of charge, while future MITx courses would charge a modest fee. Students needed at least 60 points to earn the honor code certificate.That paper appeared in Research & Practice in Assessment and is titled. Lori Breslow and five co-authors report that the course consisted of video lectures, problem sets, online labs and forums. The course generated a rich data set on how learners used the platform. The first stage of the research measured the time students spent on each tool and the second stage aimed to build a profile of who the students were and how their background and capability related to achievement and persistence.Piotr Mitros and colleagues, including Agarwal, wrote Teaching electronic circuits online: Lessons from MITx’s 6.002x on edX, which describes the online course as content-identical to the sophomore-level Circuits and Electronics course taken by residential MIT students. Those who managed to accumulate enough points were issued an honor code certificate by MITx.After its initial spring 2012 run, 6.002x was offered again in fall 2012 and spring 2013, according to the above-mentioned study by Breslow and colleagues. Class Central reported that edX shut down the original platform on March 15, 2017, and moved the roughly 155,000 original registrants to an invitation-only alumni version of the course.
Article Summary: MITx opened its first course, 6.002x: Circuits and Electronics, on March 5, 2012. Nearly 155,000 people from more than 160 countries signed up for the course. MITx became edX in May 2012 and the course was shut down on March 15, 2017.

Article Title: In New Jersey, painter John Fricano built Jack and Jill’s Hill and the Three Bears’ house for his kids in 1955; Storybook Land grew to 20 acres, with 19 rides
Article Text:
Storybook Land in Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey, opened by John and Esther Fricano in 1955. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Five wooded acres in

Egg Harbor Township

and a founding in 1955

From 20 acres and 14 rides in 2015 to 19 rides on the park’s website today

Bubbles the Coaster was among Storybook Land’s rides when The Philadelphia Inquirer counted 14 rides at the park in 2015. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The Little Red Schoolhouse as the last original structure and a new attraction each year

Storybook Land is a family-owned children’s amusement park in southern New Jersey, on a highway that was once the main route for families heading to the shore. The park is built around fairy tales and nursery rhymes, with small cottages, storybook characters, shaded paths and rides sized for young children. Unlike the large theme parks built around big rides, it was designed for very young visitors. It began as the project of a local house painter, who built its first attractions himself and it is still run by his family across several generations.John Fricano, an Army veteran and house painter and his wife Esther established Storybook Land on a five-acre wooded lot in Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey and the park’s website dates its founding to 1955. The Philadelphia Inquirer places the opening in July of that year and reports that admission was 75 cents, with two simple rides for visitors. Some of the attractions Fricano built himself include Little Red Schoolhouse, Old Woman’s Shoe and Jack and Jill’s Hill. NJ Monthly also lists the Three Bears House among the attractions. In a 2015 interview with The Philadelphia Inquirer, their granddaughter Jessica Fricano said her grandparents saw that there was little for children to do and that the park began as a luncheonette.The park later grew from its original five acres to 20 acres, WPG Talk Radio reported. Fricano died in 2009, Roadtrippers notes. By 2015, the park had 14 rides, including Bubbles the Coaster and a miniature train ride called the J&J Railroad, the Inquirer reported. The park’s website now lists 19 rides, including the Cinderoller Coaster, a pumpkin-coach ride introduced for the 2025 season.The same 2015 Inquirer report said Jessica Fricano was running the park with her father, John Fricano Jr., her brother and her aunt. A long-time staff member told NJ Monthly the park is designed for children between ages 1 and 8.Little of the park’s original construction remains, but its approach has stayed largely the same. In an earlier feature, Roadtrippers reported that the Little Red Schoolhouse is the only original structure still standing and that the family adds at least one new attraction a year while occasionally feeling pressure to chase the latest ride. Among the additions it described was a Robin Hood statue brought from a park in New York and restored for Storybook Land. The park’s website says it operates from spring through December, with ticketed events at Halloween and Christmas toward the end of the year.
Article Summary: Storybook Land in Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey, opened in July 1955. John Fricano, an Army veteran and house painter and his wife Esther established the park on a five-acre wooded lot. By 2015, the park had 14 rides, including Bubbles the Coaster and a miniature train ride called the J&J Railroad. The park’s website now lists 19 rides, with a pumpkin-coach ride introduced for the 2025 season.

Article Title: Afghan returnees face police raids, arbitrary detention in Pakistan's KP after emergency: Report
Article Text:
Emergency in Imran Khan's bastion, fresh fears for Afghan returnees in Pakistan

Afghan nationals recently deported from Pakistan have reported a rise in arbitrary detentions, midnight raids on homes and financial extortion in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following the military-backed Shehbaz Sharif government's imposition of governor’s rule and a state of emergency in the province, as news agency ANI cited TOLO News report.Returnees said daily life had become increasingly difficult, with Pakistani police frequently searching their homes and restricting their freedom of movement. Several deportees alleged that they were being detained on flimsy pretexts and that law enforcement personnel were demanding bribes in exchange for their release.Mohammad Rahman, an Afghan returnee, told TOLO News that his family had moved from Punjab to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa during former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan's tenure in search of better living conditions.However, he said the situation had deteriorated sharply after Islamabad declared an emergency and imposed governor's rule, leaving refugees afraid to step outside for fear of arbitrary arrest and extortion.Another deportee, Sohail Khan, said authorities were conducting raids on residential properties at night while targeting and intimidating refugees in local markets during the day to extract money. Displaced families also recounted being picked up from their workplaces and subjected to humiliating treatment before being deported.The reported crackdown comes as nearly 27,000 Afghan refugees have returned to Afghanistan through the Torkham border terminal over the past three months. Officials at the Omari Temporary Settlement near Torkham said administrative arrangements, including 12 dedicated support committees, remain in place to provide essential assistance and manage a possible increase in arrivals.Meanwhile, efforts to resettle returning Afghans are continuing. The Taliban-led ministry of urban development and housing said more than 74,000 residential plots had been distributed to returning families across 22 provinces.The ministry added that land had been allocated across 27 dedicated townships, with 37 master development plans formally approved to support the reintegration of returnees.The Munir-Sharif duo imposed a state of emergency and governor’s rule in Pakistan’s northwestern province, a stronghold of jailed former PM Imran Khan’s party, PTI.
Article Summary: Afghan nationals recently deported from Pakistan report rise in arbitrary detentions, midnight raids on homes and financial extortion. Comes after military-backed Shehbaz Sharif government's imposition of governor’s rule and a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Article Title: Pakistan reopens Iran border after week-long halt to commercial traffic
Article Text:
Following a week-long closure due to security threats, Pakistan has reopened the Gabd-Rimdan border crossing with Iran.

Security concerns preceded reopening

Pakistan has resumed cross-border trade with Iran through a major border point in Balochistan after a seven-day shutdown disrupted cargo movement, left transporters stranded and raised concerns about LPG availability as winter approaches.Commercial traffic restarted on Saturday at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing in Gwadar district, Dawn reported. Officials permitted the movement of import and export consignments carrying consignment notes issued on or before October 16. according to the news agency PTI.Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, head of the Gwadar chamber of commerce and industry, confirmed that the crossing, also called Gate 250, was operational again.Kalmati said trucks and other vehicles carrying commercial goods were now permitted to travel in both directions between Pakistan and Iran.Welcoming the reopening, he said it would offer relief to traders and transport operators who had been unable to move their cargo during the closure. The restoration of supplies could also help address Pakistan's LPG shortage and ease pressure on rising food and energy costs.The crossing was shut on October 17 by Pakistan's commerce ministry, which did not publicly disclose the reason for the suspension. However, security concerns were believed to have prompted the move.The disruption affected LPG supplies at a time when demand for the fuel generally increases during the colder months.The situation worsened on Thursday when unidentified gunmen attacked trucks parked near the Gabd-Rimdan crossing. Dozens of vehicles were reportedly set ablaze, while several others sustained damage.Local authorities reviewed the security situation before allowing trade to resume on Saturday. Additional security personnel have been deployed to safeguard commercial convoys travelling through the area.The reopening also follows a visit to Iran earlier this week by Pakistan Army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who held discussions with Iranian leaders on bilateral ties and regional developments.Pakistan and Iran share a 909-km frontier between Iran's Sistan and Baluchestan province and Pakistan's Balochistan province. The border crossings are vital channels for trade and the movement of goods between the neighbouring countries.
Article Summary: Commercial traffic restarted on Saturday at the Gabd-Rimdan crossing in Gwadar district, Dawn reported. Officials permitted the movement of import and export consignments carrying consignment notes issued on or before October 16. The disruption affected LPG supplies at a time when demand for the fuel generally increases.

Article Title: 'Islamabad arming Afghans to fight anti-Pakistani insurgents': Ex-US envoy sounds alarm
Article Text:
The allegations come amid worsening ties between Islamabad and Kabul

Former US envoy Zalmay Khalilzad has sounded the alarm over reports that Islamabad is recruiting Afghans to fight anti-Pakistan insurgents, warning that relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan are likely to deteriorate further.“There have been many reports that Pakistan is arming Afghans to fight the Taliban in Afghanistan. Now there are reports that the Pakistani military is recruiting Afghans to fight against anti-Pakistan insurgents. As things currently stand, relations between #Afghanistan and #Pakistan are likely to get much worse,” Khalilzad wrote.Pakistan's information ministry on Saturday rejected Khalilzad's allegations as “baseless and misleading”, accusing him of promoting a narrative in support of the Taliban government in Afghanistan.The allegations come amid worsening ties between Islamabad and Kabul, with repeated border clashes and Pakistani airstrikes in Afghanistan adding to tensions this year.On Saturday, Pakistani forces and Afghan Taliban personnel exchanged fire at several locations along the north-western border. Pakistani security officials and state-run media said troops, backed by artillery, destroyed Taliban posts during hours of fighting in Kurram district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Pakistani officials also claimed that troops killed an unspecified number of Pakistani Taliban militants attempting to cross into Pakistan from eastern Afghanistan. Kabul did not immediately comment on the clashes.Pakistan has accused Afghanistan of providing sanctuary to leaders and fighters of the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which is separate from but closely allied with the Afghan Taliban. Kabul has denied the allegations. The continuing violence has further strained relations between the two countries.
Article Summary: Zalmay Khalilzad warns that relations between Pakistan and Afghanistan are likely to deteriorate further. The allegations come amid worsening ties between Islamabad and Kabul. On Saturday, Pakistani forces and Afghan Taliban personnel exchanged fire at several locations along the north-western border.

Article Title: 'Pak defeated, cannot fight us': Baloch rebels launch fresh strike; several killed
Article Text:
The group also claimed to have taken control of the Muzhani police station

The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has claimed responsibility for a series of strikes against Pakistani security forces, alleging that its fighters killed a Military Intelligence (MI) captain and several personnel of the Pakistan Army’s Special Services Group (SSG) during its ongoing Operation Almas.In a press release issued by its spokesperson, Major Gwahram Baloch, the separatist group claimed that Pakistani forces had suffered significant human and material losses at multiple locations and were forced to retreat following clashes. The BLF, as cited by news agency ANI said that the operation was continuing on several fronts with “full intensity and success”.Videos purportedly showing the ongoing violence have also surfaced. In one clip, a woman is heard saying, “Pakistan is defeated now & and cannot fight us”, as gunfire continues in the background. Another video showed a woman firing what appeared to be an assault rifle.The BLF further claimed that its fighters had overrun the main camp of the Frontier Works Organization (FWO) and hoisted the organisation’s flag at Gwadar Zero Point, describing the development as evidence of its advances during the operation.The group also claimed to have taken control of the Muzhani police station, seizing official weapons and military equipment. It alleged that a police official was killed during the confrontation.In a separate incident in Gubd, the BLF said its fighters attacked a convoy of Pakistani security forces, destroying an army vehicle and killing or injuring several personnel travelling in it. The group also claimed that its fighters had taken control of the police checkpoint at Gubd Cross.
Article Summary: The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has claimed responsibility for a series of strikes against Pakistani security forces. The group alleges that its fighters killed a Military Intelligence (MI) captain and several personnel of the Pakistan Army’s Special Services Group (SSG)

Article Title: Pakistan's elite want out? Khawaja Asif flags bureaucrats' alleged exit plans to foreign shores
Article Text:
File photo: Pakistan defence minister Khwaja Asif

Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has questioned the loyalty of senior bureaucrats, alleging that several government officials planned to settle abroad while serving the country, according to a report by Pakistan's Express Tribune.In a post on X, Asif said Pakistan had capable and honest bureaucrats, but alleged that many officials had made Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and other European countries their permanent homes over the past several years.He claimed some officers had prepared for their relocation under a deliberate plan while employed by the Pakistani government. Portugal, he said, had emerged as a destination for what he described as a bureaucratic exodus in recent years. He added that he had raised the issue on social media a few months ago.Asif said the officers whose names had surfaced in connection with the matter had held important positions and remained close to successive governments. He also alleged that an individual who facilitated permanent residency arrangements had fled after collecting substantial sums of money from several influential bureaucrats.The minister did not identify the officials or provide details to substantiate the allegations. He said troubling accounts were circulating about the matter and questioned whether senior officials who had enjoyed the privileges and respect associated with public service had remained committed to Pakistan.“Does it rise above all doubt and suspicion, or are they merely in transit?” Asif asked, questioning whether such officials viewed Pakistan as their permanent home or merely a temporary stop before settling abroad.
Article Summary: Pakistan's defence minister Khawaja Asif has questioned the loyalty of senior bureaucrats. He alleges that several government officials planned to settle abroad while serving the country. Portugal has emerged as a destination for what he described as a bureaucratic exodus in recent years. He also alleged that an individual who facilitated permanent residency arrangements had fled.

Article Title: Pakistan army officer killed in IED blast during Balochistan operation
Article Text:
Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists.

A Pakistan Army major was killed in an improvised explosive device (IED) blast during a security operation in Balochistan province, while security forces killed four terrorists in a separate operation, the military said on Monday.According to a statement issued by the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, security forces conducted operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Gwadar and Jattakabad in Kalat district on Sunday following reports of terrorist presence.During an operation in Jattakabad, the forces killed four terrorists and recovered “a large cache of arms and ammunition”, the Army said.In a separate action, security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district. During the operation, 34-year-old Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation.“Sanitisation operations will continue to eliminate any other terrorists found in the area,” the Army said.The military added that security forces and law enforcement agencies remained committed to eliminating foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism in the country.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif paid tribute to the security forces for killing the four terrorists and expressed grief over the death of the officer.“Major Wajahat Waheed sacrificed his life for the protection of our beloved homeland; the nation is proud of its brave son,” the prime minister said.Sharif also extended condolences to the officer's family and prayed for the elevation of his rank.Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, with security forces continuing operations to contain the violence.A day earlier, security forces killed eight terrorists during operations in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts.(With inputs from PTI)
Article Summary: Pakistan Army major killed in Balochistan IED blast as security forces eliminate four terrorists. Major Wajahat Waheed was killed in an IED attack while leading the operation. Security forces carried out clearance operations in the Shadi Kaur area of Pasni in Gwadar district.

Article Title: US-designated LeT terrorist dies after mysteriously falling from building in Lahore
Article Text:
LeT terrorist Chaudhary Muhammed Sarwar.

NEW DELHI: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim, one of the founding members of the outfit, died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday.The incident reminded of a similar death that had occurred in 2016 when fake currency kingpin, Javed Khanani, had died after falling from an under construction building in Karachi.Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League. He was a close aide of both Hafiz Saeed and current deputy chief Saifullah Kasuri. Sarwar's son had also died in a road accident a few months ago.It was in 2016 tha Sarwar was designated a terrorist by the US justice department who termed himself as a senior LeT memeber in Lahore active since early 2000s, holding various leadership roles in the group. At the time, he was LeT’s emir for Lahore, a position he has held since at least January 2015."As the LeT emir of Lahore, Sarwar maintains relationships with LeT’s most senior leaders. Between 2012 and 2013, Sarwar worked with LeT’s foreign affairs chief Hafiz Abdul Rahman Makki, and in early 2013, Makki asked Sarwar for money to pay for his travel within Pakistan," the US justice department had said in its statement."Sarwar had been directly involved in LeT fundraising activities and used the formal financial system in Pakistan to raise and move funds on behalf of LeT. For example, in 2008, Sarwar led delegations of businessmen to LeT facilities for the purpose of soliciting donations for the group," it added.
Article Summary: US designated Lashkar-e-Taiba terrorist Chaudhry Mohammad Sarwar alias Abu Hashim died after mysteriously falling from the fourth floor of Markaz Qudesia in Lahore Sunday. Sarwar was currently handling the finance wing and fundraising excercise in Punjab province under the garb of the outfit's political wing, Pakistan Markazi Muslim League.

Article Title: Pakistani forces kill 8 militants in Balochistan, raid hideouts as abductions rise
Article Text:
The operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas (Photo: ANI).

Pakistani security forces on Sunday reportedly killed eight militants in three intelligence-led operations across districts of Balochistan province, amid rising cases of abduction in the troubled region.The operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas, according to the Inter Service Public Relations (ISPR), the media wing of the Pakistan Army.In the Panjpai area of Quetta district, terrorists trying to set up a roadblock to disrupt local traffic were "intercepted by security forces, resulting in [the] killing of five terrorists", the ISPR said in a statement.In Nushki district, security forces stormed a hideout, and two terrorists were killed in an intense exchange of fire, the army said. Around 500 kilograms of explosives were also recovered from the terrorists during that operation. In Khuzdar district, one terrorist was killed, the ISPR added.Balochistan, which borders Afghanistan, has seen a surge in abductions and attacks on civilians and securityforces in recent years, prompting the government to step up its anti-militant operations.On Saturday, unidentified armed men hijacked a bus carrying 20 trainee police officers near Mastung, on the Quetta-Karachi highway, and took them away. Their whereabouts remain unknown.On Sunday, at least 18 workers were abducted, and another was injured when unidentified armed men attacked a marble mining site in the province. The incident happened early in the morning in the remote Naal area of Khuzdar district, police said. The attackers arrived on motorcycles and other vehicles and stormed the site.According to PTI, no insurgent group or individual has claimed responsibility for the attack.The police and the provincial government have yet to confirm the incident officially, but two police officers, speaking on condition of anonymity, said 18 workers had been taken away by the attackers. PTI reported."They came on bikes and vehicles and opened fire and then rounded up the workers present at the site and abducted 18 of them before fleeing," a police officer said.Most of those abducted came from nearby villages and areas, he added, and another worker was injured in the attack.
Article Summary: Pakistani security forces reportedly kill eight militants in three intelligence- led operations across districts of Balochistan province. Operations took place on Saturday in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts, following intelligence that the militants were hiding in those areas. On Saturday, unidentified armed men hijacked a bus carrying 20 trainee police officers.

Article Title: Pakistan’s decades of backing terror comes full circle as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa falls under emergency rule
Article Text:
The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.

Decades of militant policy and blowback

Emergency rule and the erosion of elected authority

Opposition crackdown deepens rights concerns

Tribal communities face renewed uncertainty

Pakistan’s imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on October 11 has placed the province under direct federal control. It has effectively suspended the regional administration led by imprisoned former prime minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The move, which invokes Articles 232 and 234 of the Pakistani Constitution, comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. It has also renewed questions over Pakistan’s decades-long policy of using militant groups for strategic gains. A report by news agency ANI highlights how this policy has fuelled the violence now threatening its own territory.The emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, further weakening elected authority in a province that has long borne the consequences of Pakistan’s security policies. The move follows years of political turmoil, including Khan’s imprisonment, constitutional amendments that have weakened judicial independence, and the removal of the PTI-led provincial government.The concentration of power in unelected authorities, alongside the military’s expanding role in civilian affairs, has raised concerns over the state of democracy in Pakistan, according to a report by news agency ANI.Pakistan’s security crisis has deep roots in its long-standing use of militant groups as instruments of state policy. For more than five decades, the country has pursued strategic depth through its relationship with armed groups, while distinguishing between factions considered useful and those viewed as threats.This approach has contributed to a cycle of violence that has increasingly turned inward.As stated in the report, the state has repeatedly shifted its position towards militant organisations, including groups hostile to its own security forces. During former army chief General Qamar Javed Bajwa’s tenure, cadres of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were relocated to parts of the erstwhile Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA) and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.The consequences have proved difficult to contain. Pakistan’s struggle with militancy has exposed the risks of treating armed groups as strategic assets while assuming their violence can be directed towards selected targets.Former US secretary of state Hillary Clinton captured this danger in a widely cited remark, “one cannot rear snakes in a backyard and expect them to bite only neighbours, as they will eventually turn on their keepers”.Rather than confronting the broader implications of this policy, Pakistan has continued to differentiate between militant factions it considers acceptable and those it seeks to eliminate. The resulting security failures have placed civilians, particularly in the tribal areas, at the centre of a prolonged conflict.The imposition of emergency rule marks another stage in the concentration of power within Pakistan’s security establishment. The federal intervention has effectively displaced the PTI-led provincial administration, depriving the opposition of its remaining provincial government.The move follows Khan’s incarceration and constitutional changes that have curtailed judicial independence and shielded military leadership from accountability. Critics argue that these developments have weakened the institutions meant to limit executive and military power.The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers. In the affected districts, the constitutional distinction between judicial and executive authority has reportedly been set aside, concentrating control in unelected hands.Instead of addressing the failures behind the province’s deteriorating security situation, authorities have expanded federal and military involvement in civilian administration. The move has intensified concerns that emergency powers are being used not only to manage the security crisis but also to consolidate political control.The intervention has been accompanied by a wider crackdown on the opposition. Leaders and legislators have been detained, residences raided and political demonstrations suppressed. Protesters have faced police firing, tear gas and mass arrests.The treatment of political opponents has fuelled concerns that dissent is increasingly being treated as a security threat. The use of force against protesters has also raised questions about the government’s claim that extraordinary measures are needed to restore law and order.The crackdown comes amid concerns over restrictions on reporting from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, following earlier developments in Khyber before a blanket media ban was imposed on events in the province. Such restrictions risk limiting public scrutiny of security operations and their impact on civilians.The growing concentration of authority has therefore created a parallel crisis. While the state faces a persistent militant threat, its response has further narrowed the space for political opposition and public dissent.The latest intervention has also placed additional pressure on communities that have endured years of displacement and insecurity. Past military operations, including Zarb-e-Azb and Radd-ul-Fasad, remain associated with civilian hardship and human rights concerns.Thousands of displaced families are still awaiting return and rehabilitation. For these communities, the emergency raises fears of another period of disruption, particularly as the authorities expand their control and military involvement in civilian affairs.The consequences of Pakistan’s security policies have thus extended beyond the fight against armed groups. Tribal populations have faced displacement, civilian casualties and prolonged instability, while the failure to resolve the underlying conflict has left many vulnerable to further intervention.The emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa brings these tensions into sharper focus. A state that has long relied on militant groups to pursue strategic objectives now faces the consequences of violence within its own borders. Its response, however, has centred on expanding federal control, weakening elected authority and restricting opposition activity.Rather than resolving the crisis, the latest measures risk deepening the divide between the state and the communities it claims to protect. The removal of an elected provincial government, the concentration of power in unelected institutions and the crackdown on dissent point to a broader struggle over Pakistan’s democratic future, even as the country confronts the long-term fallout of its militant policies.
Article Summary: Emergency has extended federal control across 12 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. It has effectively suspended the regional administration led by Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) It comes amid a worsening security situation and a crackdown on opposition leaders and protesters. The emergency has also raised concerns about the separation of powers.

Article Title: Pakistan plans Moon landing by 2035, expands space cooperation with China
Article Text:
Pakistan sets 2035 Moon landing target as space programme expands, minister says (representative image)

First Pakistani astronaut to travel to China’s space station

Pakistan-China cooperation extends to lunar exploration

Space education and proposed museum

India’s space roadmap: From Gaganyaan to a Moon landing

Pakistan aims to land on the Moon by 2035 as it expands its space programme, planning minister Ahsan Iqbal said on Sunday, announcing that the country's first astronaut would embark on a space mission from China on November 25.Addressing the concluding ceremony of World Space Week 2026 in Narowal district of Punjab province, Iqbal said cooperation with China would help Pakistan advance its space exploration ambitions.Pakistan’s “first astronaut will embark on a space mission from China’s space centre on November 25, while the country aims to achieve a lunar landing by 2035,” he said, according to news agency PTI.The minister highlighted the growing role of space technology in agriculture, communications, climate monitoring, education and national security. He stressed that scientific research and space exploration were important for technological advancement.The upcoming mission is part of wider cooperation between Pakistan and China in space science and technology. According to Reuters, two Pakistani candidates, pilots Khurram Daud and Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, have been undergoing training in China, with one expected to be selected for the flight.The selected astronaut will serve as a payload specialist aboard China's Tiangong space station, conducting scientific experiments rather than operating the spacecraft, Reuters reported last month.Pakistan's space agency, the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (SUPARCO), signed an agreement with the China Manned Space Agency in February 2025 to prepare a Pakistani astronaut for the mission, according to The Express Tribune.The two candidates had been training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Centre in Beijing, learning spacecraft systems, Mandarin and the physical demands of spaceflight.The mission is expected to last about a week.
